This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific "smoothing" space of Barron functions, we establish that certain overparameterized neural networks achieve nearly optimal accuracy. The constraints on the smoothing space and node weights are meticulously evaluated using functional analysis and numerical methods. When the potential is uniform, we establish that the ground state belongs to the smoothing space, leading to the discovery that net overparameterization can lead to nearly optimal accuracy. Furthermore, we introduce a condition on the Laplacian that contributes to our findings for non-uniform potentials.

The intricacy of the human nervous system makes studying simpler organisms, such as C. Elegans, a more feasible option. With a well-understood behavioural and structural biology and a functional brain model already established, C. Elegans serves as an ideal model for testing simulation and modelling techniques that aim to mimic brain activity. In our research, we designed a neural network-based model using a deep learning framework to analyse the behaviour of C. Elegans based on sensory information. We built a network to learn the connections within the beast's neural framework by training it with a corpus of real-world data, then used it to predict its behaviour in unknown situations. We also developed an algorithm to discover the most significant inputs driving C. Eegans' behaviour and found that its sensory organs respond to a broad array of inputs. We not only validated our findings with statistical analysis but also compared them with the results of existing research into C. Eegans' nervous system. Overall, our model was very accurate and successful in understanding how C. Eegans responds to different stimuli.

A novel, straightforward sorting method is applied to permutations: repeatedly divide the largest element by the largest remaining element until a single number remains. At each step, record the height of the remaining permutation. These heights form a hierarchical order known as the Rauzy induction graph. While initially used in multidimensional counting, this concept has been discovered by others under the name multi-iteration. In the case of permutations, the induction graph is a rooted binary tree with a limited number of common configurations. By identifying these rare patterns, we're able to show that the heights follow a chi-squared distributed pattern. With this, we're able to derive a more efficient description of multi-iteration, achieve a detailed understanding of multi-iteration's behavior in the limit of large permutations, and make a precise prediction regarding the time it takes for multi-iteration.

A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) is defined by a group G and subgroup H, 
with every irreducible character of H resulting in a multiplicity-free 
character of G. Specifically, we identify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, 
p) when p is a prime number.

This research delves into electromagnetic characteristics of $S$-wave isoscalar pentaquark states, identified previously, in terms of transition form factors and radial form factors. Our goal is to gain insights that can aid in uncovering the internal structures of these states through experimental processes such as two-photon fusion. To achieve this, we have created interrelated potential models for five-body systems consisting of four quarks and one gluon, based on a specific linear potential model with Coulombic quark-quark interactions. We employ the Lüscher boundary condition to obtain pole positions for pentaquark states, and our results for ground-state pole positions are consistent with those obtained using the variational principle. We further utilize the resonance eigenstates to examine the contributions of individual constituents to the mass deficits of these resonances. Our empirical findings suggest a large spatial extent of these resonances, as well as a roughly estimated net gluon content of about 0.55, and our predictions for the transition form factors of these resonances have the potential to be validated through future experiments.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This research examines the scattering theory for a cubic, spatially varying Schrödinger equation with an inverse square potential: $iu_t + \Delta u - \frac{a}{|x|^2}u = \lambda |x|^{-b} |u|^2u$ with $a > -\frac14$ and $0 < b < 1$ in 3D space. The paper establishes global solvability and scattering in the energy space $H^1_a(\mathbb R^3)$ for all initial conditions in the defocusing scenario, whereas for the focusing scenario, it proves scattering for data below a threshold by leveraging a virial/Morawetz method.

Consider an N-station network where K_N customers reside, each station functioning as a./M/∞ queue with service rate mu, and following an SIS model, where customers transition between infected and susceptible states upon interaction within the stations. When departing, they move randomly to another station. In addition to the interaction, susceptible customers become infected with rate alpha times the number of infected customers, while infected customers recover and revert to susceptible with rate beta. In the infinite-station limit, we find parameters that support an equilibrium regime where the disease thrives. Several key findings emerge about this equilibrium system - it's rare, it exhibits a sharp phase transition, and displays mean-field behavior. We've derived analytic expressions for mean rates of susceptible and infected states and demonstrated the convergence of these mean rates to the limit S_N and I_N as N increases. We've also obtained a significant result - the disease phase's lower boundary is asymptotically guarded by the minimal value of N/π. Given this critical finding, we can now deduce that I_N, rescaled by the stationary distribution, will converge to a limit as N increases.

Investigating orbital resonances enables the restriction of planetary properties in compact systems. The early K-type star K2-138, hosting four known planets, is an ideal case to analyze through this approach. Its planetary properties were further constrained by analyzing the light curve for potential transit signals, a procedure that previous studies failed to conduct. By assuming a gas planetary system, our results indicate a chain of 3:2 mean motion resonances between the planets. From synthetic light curves analysis, our results show a 95% likelihood of a 5.097-day period planet and a 99% likelihood of a 8.920-day period planet. Additionally, our results provide 1σ and 2σ confidence intervals for the planets' orbital periods and masses. Orbit simulations confirm that this planetary system undergoes a chain of resonances with a 99% likelihood of a stable configuration in its early stage with a Jupiter-like planet within a 21-24 day period range. However, our results show a 95% likelihood of a stable configuration in its later stage with a Black Hole-like object.

We establish connections between the Gelfand--Graev modules for central covers, the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial of the Arnold--Brieskorn manifold, and the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality via a permutation representation of the Weyl group, which governs these three objects.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas.

Using advanced computer simulations, researchers studied the molecular structure of water in hexagonal ice (Ih) and low-density amorphous ice (LDA) at low temperatures under high pressure conditions. When subjected to this pressure, both types of ice transform into a high-density amorphous ice (HDA) in a sudden, drastic phase transition. An analysis of the structural changes used the local order metric (LOM), which measures the degree of organization within the material by comparing simulated X-ray density measurements to actual X-ray density measurements of the same material. Notably, ice IV forms under extremely high pressure conditions and is distinguished from LDA ice by its higher local organization, while ice HDA regains some of this organization when transformed into ice V at high pressure. An accompanying phase diagram illustrates the various phase transitions that occur when low-density amorphous ice is subjected to high pressure.

A set of experiments utilized the STM instrument, employing a probe tip to investigate sample surfaces by tracking tunnelling currents. These studies included (1) utilizing STM to map the atomic structure of Highly Oriented Pyrolytic Graphite's (HOPG) surface to calculate its lattice constant, (2) employing STS mode to investigate the electronic structure of Gold (Au) Auger levels in Gold nanoparticles and the energy levels of the STM tip itself, and (3) examining Iron (Fe) nanoparticle work functions under varying environments. Results indicated that (1) the lattice constant measured for HOPG was $2.45 \pm 0.01 \mathbf{ \hat{A}}$, which aligns with known values and also literature findings on the lattice constant of HOPG using STM; (2) CURIE temperature ($\mathbf{ T_{C}}$) was found for Gold nanoparticle environmental dependence; and (3) under distinct environmental conditions, the variance in work functions of Iron nanoparticles was observed to be roughly twice that of Gold nanoparticles. These studies explored environmental dependencies using STM and STS techniques.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of a scale-free network, as evidenced by the distributed nature of community structures and a varying degree of computational complexity among its constituent elements.

In situ data from the heliosphere is often used for observational analysis but produces complex time-series information that's more effectively interpreted as sound. Audification is an informative way to analyze oscillatory data, providing an intuitive understanding of large-scale structures and long-term variations in space. By applying this method to heliospheric data, large-scale objects like the heliospheric field's outer boundary, the bow shock, and the outer heliospheric field itself become audible at specific frequencies. This technique allows new objects to be identified and existing objects re-identified through the 'audification' of historical spacecraft data.

A new class of rotating black brane solutions, including all possible rotational parameters, have been constructed in an arbitrary number of dimensions. These rotating black branes are flat in topology at their horizons, yet due to the influence of the dilaton field, they do not conform to either flat or (anti)-de Sitter asymptotic behaviors. We've analyzed their physical properties by applying a method that uses the counterterm, which was inspired by AdS/CFT correspondence. This has allowed us to calculate mass and angular momentum, and we have determined the temperatures, electric potentials, and entropies at the horizons, thereby enabling the calculation of thermal stability. It has been found that under certain conditions, these solutions can become unstable for certain values of the dilaton-electromagnetic coupling constant, denoted alpha. We have also explored nonrotating limitations and discovered that these solutions, when applied to four-dimensional spacetime, correlate with the work by Ayoub for charged rotating black holes. Furthermore, we have successfully demonstrated the application of the mass-temperature relationship. Finally, we have examined the thermal velocity of these solutions and have identified a range of temperatures and velocities for various spacetime parameters.

In the era of artificial intelligence, computational advancements in text analysis are crucial. Multiple systems have been created to process text across various languages. Despite the considerable advancements, these systems still struggle with text comprehension, essentially treating text as data rather than knowledge. We introduce a novel text representation framework inspired by human memory, acknowledging that text is declarative and would benefit from structural organization to facilitate efficient computation. We utilize long-term episodic memory to store text information accumulated over time, maintaining it in an organized manner, eliminating redundancy, and retaining temporal relationships. To facilitate understanding of individual words, we apply Wordnet, simulating semantic networks in short-term memory. Our approach is characterized by simplicity, flexibility, and effectiveness, as demonstrated by its application to a range of text processing tasks including language identification, feature extraction, and sentiment analysis.

For any real number q, such that its absolute value is less than one, we explore the universal C*-algebra derived from a q-canonical commutation relation *-algebra. Fock space, possessing the C*-norm, is proven to be the smallest normable representation. In the case where q equals i, this study aligns with the findings of Arv\'e and Lieberman regarding the universal C*-algebra of canonical commutation relations.

A small-step operational semantics in a programming language breaks down computations into discrete, indivisible steps, directly reflecting how the language is implemented.  A previous semantics of GP 2 is incomplete because its loop and branching commands utilize big-step operations.  This paper presents a new small-step operational semantics for GP 2, effectively capturing the nature of divergent computations.  Achieving small-step definitions for all of GP 2's commands requires integrating a host graph stack and associated operations into the transition relation.  By incorporating a graph stack into the transition relation, GP 2's reduction is represented as a sequence of small steps.  Notably, this formulation does include reducible configurations involving divergent computations.  In contrast to a prior approximation of GP 2's semantics, this formulation does exclude configurations involving non-terminating evaluations, but it is complete and includes all relevant goals and contexts.

We generated theoretical predictions for the disk of TW Hydrae using different
scenarios. One model involves the disk's destruction through photoevaporation,
producing an inner emission gap. Another option is a disk with an external
emission gap created by the dissolution of an outer disk. A third possibility is
a disk fragmented into multiple separate emitters. We observed that this last
scenario aligns with the disk's structure observed in 30 Arietis, although the
discrete dust emission in this system has a more natural explanation as
undisturbed protoplanetary material. We analyzed the emission from the three
theoretical models of TW Hydrae and found that the one with an outer emission
gap best fits the emission profile it generates. The emission patterns of the
other two scenarios do not as closely match observed data from TW Hydrae. We
observed that the disk of TW Hydrae has an emission profile that does not have
two distinct emission components separated by a gap. This suggests that the
disk is in a stage where it transitioned from having an outer emission gap to
disintegrating into multiple small disks or disks around multiple stars. We
observed that the emission levels of the middle emission component in this
model are within expected levels when compared to other young stars, indicating
this type of transition might be a common stage for young stars on the path to
disintegrating into multiple small disks or disks around multiple stars. We

We address the factorization of specific polynomial variants by deriving new solutions for expressions involving Chebyshev polynomials of the third and fourth kinds. The proof method leverages previous work by Wolfram on factorizing variants of Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kinds. Additionally, we establish that minimal polynomials based on cosine values do not yield factorizations for certain Chebyshev polynomial variants of the fifth and sixth kinds.

This research assesses the feasibility of time and time-frequency features-based classifiers in distinguishing between internal faults and other transient phenomena - such as magnetizing inrush and overexcitation - occurring in Indirect Symmetrical Phase Angle Regulating Transformers. Once the transformer's faulty unit is pinpointed through current transformation, the features are extracted from the post-transformation currents and fed into a multi-class classifier. Performance metrics, including confusion matrix assessment, classification error rates, and likelihood ratios, are used to evaluate the performance of various classifiers including SVM, BN, and GTL. Among these, the GTL classifier exhibits the highest accuracy, with a likelihood ratio greater than 20 separating internal faults from non-faults including both non-internal faults and inrush/overexcitation events. Additionally, the GTL classifier outperforms other classifiers, with a likelihood ratio greater than 45 distinguishing between three types of non-faults/inrush/overexcitation and internal faults. Consequently, the proposed method's success suggests that the GTL classifier is an optimal choice for detecting internal faults in ISPARTs under non-faults/inrush/overexcitation events.

The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in the design of hybrid precoders. To fill this gap, we develop the first integrated design of analog transmit precoders and digital receive combiners for multicasting in mmWave systems. We propose an iterative algorithm which combines both analog and digital processing, and confirm its convergence. Notably, our results show that multicast beamforming can be beneficial or detrimental to overall spectral efficiency, contingent on the number of receive antennas. Moreover, our approach yields an approximate 40% increase in multicast capacity at a fixed unicast rate, but also results in a diminished single-user unicast rate. We observe that using a part of the mmWave band for multicasting may not be beneficial if the remainder is not utilized efficiently in other applications. We confirm the practical applicability of our approach by testing it on various mmWave channel models.

A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined by two growth patterns: one growing and the other shrinking, both following the form 2 raised to a linearly increasing exponent. In this study, techniques are developed to detect a unique type of growth in groups that interact with root trees, characterized by their rate exceeding the exponential rate. Specifically, this near-exponential growth is proven in specific root tree groups known as Branson groups and in a broader root tree group family called the Braun-Bremner group. Interestingly, these groups support growth rates both below and above the exponential rate. Additionally, this study establishes connections between these groups and partial automorphisms of local structures, specifically partial actions on a complement of a sphere in a vector space, via a novel approach that generalizes the 'inclusion-exclusion' principle. One of the key outcomes is that Branson groups can be understood as controlling a set of partial automorphisms with a small sphere of restriction, corresponding to 3-dimensional case scenarios.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving along a single axis. Utilizing a direct approach within the space of functions that are square-integrable on the graph, we establish that certain modified eigenfunctions, which are comprised of eigenvectors and a singular cutoff function, serve as a suitable observability measure. Consequently, we demonstrate the exponential stability of the system using an L^2 norm as a metric. Notably, the chosen cutoff function is singular at the point where the three branches converge, thus showing that it's possible to achieve stability without any additional regularity constraints on the eigenvectors at this critical point.

Predictions for nuclear masses are achieved through Bayesian neural networks by first understanding the patterns in a set of nuclear data and then using this information to make accurate mass predictions for previously unknown nuclei. A new mass model has been created by analyzing the M\"{o}ller interaction potential and its related forces, formulating a new method based on the Bayesian neural network approach. This new approach is evaluated on a comprehensive set of nuclear data, including over 1500 measured nuclear masses, 29 known beta-decay chains, three known chain segments with ten or more decay states, seventeen thousand theoretical nuclear masses, and 302 very heavy isotomes. A very accurate prediction of nuclear masses is achieved with this new model, well within the 100 keV threshold for most mass regions. This new model also stands in high agreement with the M\"{o}ller mass formula, particularly for well-known isotopes. Furthermore, the new model displays high accuracy in predicting nuclear mass structure, including specific shell energies, magic number alignments, and the most heavy or light isotopes. A new method for validating Bayesian neural networks has been created based on statistical analysis, including the use of posterior uncertainty, prior data sets, and the Bernoulli inequality. This new approach identifies potential inaccuracies in the data or the new model, including biases in the M\"{o}ller interaction potential. A new mass model has been created for nuclear masses based on the new Bayesian neural network approach, demonstrating high accuracy well within

Superconducting qubit performance is constrained by dielectric loss. Experimental evidence sets upper limits on dielectric loss tangents, measured near 250 mK, on Emitted Epsilon-R (ε0) 10 mF capacitors. A newly developed technique for measuring dielectric loss tangents at very low temperatures involves altering qubit frequencies and measuring related effects. This method offers high sensitivity when operating at optimal conditions. Dielectric loss is calculated based on hybrid mode eigenfrequencies of Euler twists and analyzed using a complex capacitance approach. This approach reflects variations in real and imaginary components of dielectric constant. A 10 mF ε0 Epsilon-R capacitor's loss tangent was measured and evaluated based on the produced results. This method can evaluate dielectric loss at very low temperatures with high precision. Evaluation was based on the effect of real and imaginary constant variations on frequency metrics. This approach offers an in-depth understanding of dielectric properties and dielectric potential in qubit designs.

A moving dielectric interface causes a change in the path of light traveling towards it, resulting in a deviation from its straight path. This phenomenon, known as the Fresnel-Fizeau drag effect, reduces the path of light traveling towards the interface. In contrast, when light travels away from the interface, the path is increased, known as the Abraham drag effect. The nature of this effect has been debated with both models predicting the observable behavior. A new experiment was conducted to measure the optical drag effect using various gases and found that it can be described correctly using the Fresnel-Fizeau model.

This paper introduces an exact calculation method for worst-case scenario parameter realization in two-stage robust optimization problems. Unlike traditional exact algorithms, which encounter significant computational challenges for large problems, our approach leverages a specific relation between robust optimization problems in standard and robust equivalence forms. By utilizing this connection, we create an exact calculation tool, which we then apply to various reformulation techniques for tackling a broader class of robust optimization problems. Notably, we extract worst-case scenario parameter realizations for problems with box-constrained uncertainty sets in a finite time, without relying on approximate solutions from trust region algorithms. Moreover, we extend our findings to a class of robustly distributed and flexible optimization problems. Numerical experiments confirm the efficiency and scalability of our algorithm, which remains modular, allowing it to be paired with any available reformulation method.

The understanding of socioeconomic status has evolved significantly, with various indicators providing insight into a region's diversity. A novel approach for classifying socioeconomic status in large urban areas utilizes data from real estate transactions and traffic cameras. Our method generates a comprehensive and precise classification system that accounts for geographic variability at a fine scale. This is achieved by leveraging the capabilities of deep learning models, specifically convolutional neural networks, in handling diverse datasets and identifying patterns. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, particularly in relation to the accuracy and overall cost of the classification model. This approach has the potential to be applied to multiple datasets with a low cost of data entry and acquisition, making it a valuable tool for urban planning and urban mobility applications.

The development of pattern extraction algorithms helps gain valuable insights into ever-growing datasets by translating recurring data features into simplified representations. These algorithms are now applied to extensive datasets, generating a wealth of information that requires advanced visualization to fully understand. New techniques and tools need to be designed to keep up with the increasing complexity and volume of the extracted patterns. This research introduces a visualization model called LDA-Vis, which makes it possible to work with thousands of patterns derived from document analysis. A comprehensive evaluation of the implementation and effectiveness of this model is conducted through user studies on both collaborative and individual bases. Our analysis of the results demonstrates the usability and advantages of LDA-Vis in comparison to existing pattern analysis tools.

Deep learning models' success in graph spaces is further bolstered by graph neural networks (GNNs). In contrast to their traditional deep learning counterparts, GNNs' transfer learning capabilities remain underexplored despite growing interest. Our research reveals the effectiveness of transfer learning in GNNs and highlights how both source tasks and chosen GNN architectures impact learnable knowledge. By employing real-world and synthetic data within node and graph classification frameworks, we introduce a general methodology for transfer learning experimentation, along with an innovative method for creating synthetic graph classification tasks. Notably, we found GNNs can retain up to 60% of their learned parameters and achieve substantial performance gains through transfer learning.

A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns that connect users to similar items. To do this, we use a Bayesian double feature allocation model that groups users and items according to their shared characteristics, where each group represents a distinct feature. The Indian buffet process (IBP) facilitates the linkage between users, items, and features. The approach trains rating effects specifically for each feature, thus making predictions about user preferences. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated using the MovieLens dataset, where it accurately predicts user preferences for previously unrated items. Additionally, our solution incorporates a semi-consensus Monte Carlo method to speed up the system, yielding notable improvements in both prediction accuracy and scalability.

One of the key problems originating from communication complexity, known as the promise set disjointness problem, holds crucial importance in the realm of algorithmic research. The fundamental idea revolves around determining whether a subset of elements, drawn from a 1 to d numerical range, is disjoint from a subset of elements, also drawn from a 1 to d numerical range. The analysis of the promise set disjointness scenario encompasses two distinct hypotheses, namely the "highly likely" and "almost always likely" cases, which are evaluated individually. The "highly likely" case examines a scenario where a majority of possible sub-sets of elements do not have any element overlap, and the goal is to develop algorithms for this scenario using elements from 1 to d numerical range with a goal of achieving a 1/poly(d) error rate, and the required memory for this is proven to be optimally $O(d/ log d)$ using a concept known as the "entropic idea". The "almost always likely" case, on the other hand, assesses a scenario where a majority of possible sub-sets of elements do not have more than k element overlap, and the goal is to develop algorithms for this scenario using elements from 1 to d numerical range with a goal of achieving a 1/d^3 error rate for k=d^(3-beta) for any value of beta greater than 1/4, and the required memory for this is proven to be optimally of the form of the

We investigate the momentum dependence of the static magnetic susceptibility χ(q) within the paramagnetic phase of Heisenberg magnets, particularly in relation to its critical behavior within the nonlinear sigma model (NLSM) at dimensions 2 < d < 4. By expanding up to the first order of 1/N, where N is the number of spin components, we discover a proportionality between χ(q) and [q^2 + (1/N)^(-2)]^{-1 + η/2}, with ξ representing the correlation length, q being the momentum measured relative to the magnetic wave vector, and a universal scaling function describing the deviations from standard Landau-Ginzburg behavior. The scaling function is analogous to previously established results, with f(x >> 1) being proportional to (2B_{Z}^2 + (1/N)^2)(1 + (1/2)x^2(1/N^2)^(-1))); however, for the scaling parameter B_{Z}, we determine it as (N/Z)J_{d/N} with J being the exchange energy. Furthermore, the momentum dependence of the thermal mass of spin-waves also exhibits an analogous form.

A monolithically integrated multi-grating system has been proposed to establish a connection between isolated atoms and photonic chip technology, enabling the precise direction and convergence of lasers towards the chip surface to capture, manipulate and analyze single Rubidium atoms. This includes an optical dipole trap formed by the intersection of two laser beams of 850 nm, creating a pattern of traps with diameters of around 2.7 micrometers per atom, which guides a probe laser of 780 nm to stimulate and detect atomic fluorescence while delivering a second laser of 610 nm to cool the atoms. This design offers a compact and self-contained solution for forthcoming single-photon nanowavefront manipulators that will enable the fusion of single-photon processes with chip-based technology to study single-photon interactions and explore nonlinear phenomena.

Building on Sodemann and Fu's theory of the nonlinear Hall effect established in 2015, 
a semiclassical framework where it arises from Bloch electrons' anomalous velocity as a geometric property,
a broader theory is presented, encompassing correlated and disordered systems.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the velocity-controlled vertical take-off and rendezvous (VTVR) aircraft. Our approach to tackling the resulting nonlinear system is a combined strategy involving quasi-Newton methods and interior-point optimization.

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism.

Two-dimensional semiconducting devices are highly sought after for their potential to overcome the significant power consumption of traditional 2D materials while facilitating high carrier mobilities and tunable band gaps. Transition-metal dichalcogenides have garnered significant attention due to their unique electronic properties, which can be modified by adjusting their layer thickness. Focusing on the 1T-TMD family, we demonstrate that these materials in a free-standing and stretched configuration can exhibit nodeless, anisotropic energy bands with inherently high carrier velocities and non-Abelian lattice interactions. Our results show that these properties are consistent across different sizes and stiffness values, leading to the presence of Dirac points at high velocities. The experimental verification of these properties is possible through tweaking 1T-TMDs within an oxide substrate, resulting in a device with exceptionally high carrier velocities similar to those observed in graphene. Furthermore, our findings suggest that such materials can be used to create new reference systems to inform the development of 2D materials and semiconducting devices, including heterostructures that combine different 2D materials.

A widely used mathematical framework, known as delta lenses, enables the modelling and designing of bidirectional transformations between different models. In this study, Fong et al's recent discoveries have motivated the development of an advanced delta lens framework. A key innovation within this enhanced framework involves incorporating learning capabilities into the delta lenses. A key theoretical advancement involves proving the natural inclusion of a specific category. A crucial practical application within this framework involves providing an advanced, refined form of point-wise optimisation known as point optimisation. Aims and objectives have been achieved through a systematic incorporation of Fong et al's discoveries, thereby allowing the definition of a category that includes, amongst others, the following: exclusive and extensible transformations, a type of super composition known as mixing, both asymmetrical and symmetrical lenses, a concept known as the underlying data, as well as incorporating both partial and probabilistic maps. It is demonstrated that incorporating learning capabilities facilitates point-wise optimisation. A key practical value of this framework involves supporting, amongst others, the kinds of transformations that involve linear transformations as well as the kinds of transformations known as natural transformations, such as the kinds of transformations, comprising: exclusive and extensible transformations, a type of super composition known as mixing, both asymmetrical and symmetrical lenses, a concept known as the underlying data, as well as incorporating both partial and probabilistic maps. This research focuses on developing estimates for oscillatory integrals with stationary phase. Building upon previous work by Alazard, Burq, and Zuily, we significantly refine the regularity conditions necessary for phase and amplitude functions. Moreover, we extend the analysis to a new class of oscillatory integrals where the phase and amplitude functions depend on an oscillation parameter. A novel approach utilizing wave packet decomposition transforms the analysis from an exponential decay to a geometric disjointness property, reducing the sensitivity to the smoothness of phase and amplitude functions. This geometric insight enables us to establish a uniform stationary phase estimate with weaker regularity assumptions.

A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gas dynamics lies in determining the steady-state solution of the Boltzmann equation efficiently. The conventional iteration method often achieves a steady-state solution in a few iterations, but its efficiency severely declines in the near-continuum regime where the Boltzmann equation has to be approximately solved due to the complexity of exact Boltzmann collision operators. Our work involves the application of an iteration parameter in the balance equation, allowing a near-continuum solution to be accurately achieved in a manner independent of the number of particles. This efficient near-continuum solution makes it possible to easily switch between solutions of the Boltzmann equation and its fluid dynamic models.

The Horizon-10T collaboration has collected a vast dataset amounting to approximately $4.5\times10^9$ minimum ionising particle events, obtained via a vacuum chamber technique with high sensitivity, resulting in a 30-fold increase in sensitivity compared to its previous version. Utilising a combination of advanced AI and human analysis on detailed images, scientists have developed an advanced detection system that boosts efficiency while minimizing false positives. Using a cutting-edge analytic tool, researchers have identified the "Peak Bunch" phenomenon which presents multiple peaks at intervals of around 1.6 mm, separated by 2.3 standard deviations, and further resolves each peak into smaller sub-peaks at remarkably small scales of around 0.3 mm dispelling previous theories of a single peak as solely based on electron multiplication. Moreover, by examining the spatial distribution of this "Peak Bunch" along with intricate patterns of contrasting signs, researchers have confirmed a clustering origin of this phenomenon. Last but not the least, by dissecting the time sequence of this "Peak Bunch"'s creation, researchers have learned that it appears around 1 mm from the central chamber area and further evolves over time with detectable signs near the chamber's surface. All these newly uncovered details at Horizon-10T not only increase our understanding but also open up new avenues for research on this unique phenomenon present in numerous experimental setups around the world.

The latest CMS updates reveal preliminary findings based on complete datasets from 2011 and 2012 in a 125 GeV Higgs-like boson analysis. Analyzing 7 TeV and 8 TeV data totalling 24.7 inverse femtobarns, observations showed a 125.4 GeV signal that aligns with the Standard Model at 78% of expectations, statistically confirmed at 3.2σ against the background alone. Additionally, cross-validation based on cut-based analysis found the Higgs signal occurring at 124.5 GeV and also at 1.11 times the Standard Model expectations, statistically confirmed at 3.9σ.

We introduce a concept for the p-divisibility transposition of the Fourier coefficients 
of Siegel modular forms. This concept complements the Wilton result on p-divisibility for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function.

In 2002, Biss researched a type of fibration known as the rigid fibration (initially called the rigid covering fibration), exhibiting properties akin to covering spaces. This study establishes a connection between general topological spaces and their corresponding rigid fibrations. This relationship enables a commutative diagram involving homotopy groups and quasitopological homotopy groups, resulting in further significant outcomes in this domain.

The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself at ultra-low temperatures by causing fermions to occupy the same quantum state due to an unusual effect known as fermionic condensation. The possibility of achieving this condensation in ultra-cold gases was initially proposed, and since then, researchers have successfully studied it using a variety of theoretical frameworks. Theories involving three-body losses are especially crucial in the research on this topic, and in this paper, a new theoretical approach based on the density matrix formalism is presented, which takes into account the unique properties of fermionic condensates effectively. The proposed theory has been applied to a few prominent systems, such as the autoionizing mixture and the one- and two-channel Fermi superfluids, and the results show a significant correlation with existing research data. The comprehensive density matrix formalism established in this study is ready for use in the study of other loss-driven systems.

This study aims to introduce Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN) to a global audience and provide both a conceptual and computational understanding of these algorithms in addressing time-varying matrix problems. Although ZNN was initially developed in China around 2001, the majority of breakthroughs have originated from and are based in this country. ZNN has emerged as a standard method for handling time-varying matrix problems that arise in real-time computations of science, engineering, and industry. Its core strength lies in supporting online computations of accurate solutions to various nonlinear and linear matrix problems that arise in a wide range of applications, such as signal processing, control systems, nonlinear systems, and machine learning. This paper initially examines the underlying principles of ZNN algorithms before providing detailed discussions on three main types: nonlinear mapping-based ZNN, homogeneous solution-based ZNN, and homogeneous error-based ZNN. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of Homogeneous Error-based ZNN is presented, demonstrating its ability to efficiently solve time-varying linear problems in real-time. Finally, a series of numerical experiments are designed to validate the theoretical findings and showcase the efficiency and reliability of Homogeneous Error-based ZNN in real-time applications.

Achieving resistance to diverse lighting conditions is a primary goal for any advanced computer vision system. To accomplish this, our study enhances the field of view for deep neural networks using two core components from the visual processing systems of vertebrates - the bright-sensitive (rod) and the shade-sensitive (cone) pathways. We introduce a deep separation network, integrating the outputs of these pathways with the conventional RGB images to enhance network robustness against varying lighting conditions. Furthermore, our proposed approach adapts the lighting conditions for the network by learning a non-linear lighting model. We evaluate the effectiveness of our system in edge detection tasks and achieve superior performance on four benchmark datasets, outperforming several leading deep learning models.

Our team is currently developing a simulation tool to optimize the design parameters of wide-field X-ray telescopes including field of view, point source focus, and spatial resolution. To achieve this, we are utilizing a novel approach where the optimal glass prescriptions are generated using machine learning algorithms fed optimized mirror thickness profiles obtained through Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. We leverage a wavefront aberration model to accurately model the effects of sagging and aberrations in the mirror surface. Our research is progressing in conjunction with a related project that utilizes robotic control methods to refine mirror prescriptions based on pre-optimal designs. We are currently in the process of integrating all these developments into a comprehensive simulation tool.

The core of topological band theory, Bloch's theorem, is a fundamental concept in quantum materials research. Nevertheless, it is disrupted by perpendicular magnetic fields, rendering the study of strong magnetic flux challenging for topological systems. The advent of moiré materials brings this challenge to fruition: large flux through the moiré unit cell hinders application of Bloch's theorem. To overcome this limitation, an alternative formalism is established for analyzing the wave functions of moiré Hubbard models under arbitrary magnetic flux. The established formalism is applicable to both flat and non-flat bands, and it finds that the moiré Hubbard model with periodic boundary conditions experiences an integer factor of the flux inserted into the moiré unit cell. The established formalism is then applied to both trivial and non-trivial symmetry conditions. In cases of trivial symmetry, any gauge can be used, and it is observed that the Hamiltonian can be transformed into a real-space, position-dependent superlattice Hamiltonian. Conversely, in cases of non-trivial symmetry, any non-zero flux disrupts the symmetry. The established formalism is then applied to both flat and non-flat bands, and it reveals a unique set of symmetry-protected degeneracies that are modulated by the flux at a specific rate. The established formalism is finally applied to the Bernal graphene moiré model under two different symmetry conditions. Inspired by a desire to protect user privacy, we have developed a novel, stealthy communication system that allows two users to secretly share encrypted messages. Our proposed linguistic stegosystem is based on an LSTM neural network, which has previously demonstrated superior performance in natural language processing tasks. We optimized the system by fine-tuning its parameters and refining its design, and our key innovations include a new target function for training and a unique LSTM architecture. Our statistical analysis reveals that our system is secure, and we have thoroughly tested its steganographic capabilities by measuring its transmission capacity, robustness, and accuracy. The results show that our system is highly effective, achieving a transmission capacity of nearly 1000 bits per message, and maintaining a remarkably high accuracy rate.

Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment as crucial tools for determining the most cost-effective and feasible generation schedules. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of unnecessary constraints. Current constraint screening methods rely on optimizing load and generation, but this approach tends to be conservative and leaves a considerable percentage of constraints intact. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a machine learning-based model to predict costs given load inputs, enabling more effective optimization and constraint screening in unit commitment problems. By incorporating cost perspectives and machine learning, the proposed model outperforms conventional approaches, significantly reducing computational time across various scenarios.

Measurements of magnetization were performed on polycrystalline and single-crystalline 
samples of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$, under pressures of up to 2 GPa, allowing for the creation 
of a temperature-pressure phase diagram for the material. Compression was found to have a 
minor effect on the N\'eel temperature, which increases at a rate of 1.5 K/GPa. At pressures 
exceeding 1.2 GPa, the material undergoes a structural phase transition, becoming a nonmagnetic 
phase above 1.8 GPa, whereas the magnetic phase ceases to exist at low temperatures above 
this threshold. We demonstrate that this behavior is characterized by a minimal entropy 
dissipation within the nonmagnetic state, indicating that $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ is essentially 
in a Kitaev limit even at ambient pressure. We further propose that the nonmagnetic phase 
is generated by the hybridization of Ir $5d$-like waves with O $2p$-like waves, which is 
favored under higher pressure conditions. Consequently, the magnetic exchange is effectively 
abolished as these waves come from the same parity of wave functions. Moreover, an almost 
sensitive experimental observation requires very small changes in free energy which is 
natural under high-pressure conditions for observing low-temperature (Kelvin) quantum 
properties in Ir

Researchers frequently apply synthetic control techniques to determine the effects of treatment on aggregate outcomes in a specific unit by means of a weighted average of observed pre-treatment data from various non-treatment units. The weights are objectively optimized with the objective of producing post-treatment results that closely resemble those of the treated unit following the treatment's implementation. This study presents several conceptual issues surrounding the synthetic control method's use and offers perspectives on potential resolutions, specifically addressing whether the synthetic control estimation is viewable as a conventional supervised learning task and whether the weights should be regarded as estimators of their true values.

Determining similarity between structured data, especially graph structures, is a fundamental problem that has been crucial in multiple applications of data mining and machine learning. Recent advances in Gromov-Wasserstein distance have highlighted its potential to effectively capture topological and feature-based similarities while also addressing issues related to data permutations. Nevertheless, structured data are widely dispersed across different organizations and can only be accessed on a limited basis due to concerns about privacy. To resolve this dilemma, a privacy-protecting framework has been developed that uses Gromov-Wasserstein distance to facilitate the comparison of structured data while implementing both differential privacy and a quantization technique to ensure sensitive information remains confidential. Experimental results demonstrate that while the framework sacrifices some level of data accuracy for the purpose of data privacy, it achieves this while maintaining data's overall statistical characteristics and features accurately.

The dynamics of background electron injection into a developing plasma bubble behind an extremely powerful laser beam is a multifaceted phenomenon influenced by two primary mechanisms. As an intense laser beam traverses a plasma, forming a shock-like steepened edge, these mechanisms act in tandem. Meanwhile, periodic plasma bubble oscillations along the laser beam path can either hinder or cooperate with electron injection driven by bubble expansion. Accounting for the specific characteristics of intense laser interactions with plasmas, such as nonlinear laser pulse self-steepening and plasma bubble oscillations, is essential for accurately predicting the structure and characteristics of electrons injected into the developing plasma bubble. Electron acceleration within the bubble can either be a collective or a individual process. Traces of this complex dynamics include tiny filament formation, electron vacuum plasmon, electron recircation due to bubble oscillations, and a trident-like process that occurs when a laser beam travels through a thin target, leading to forward, backward, and a central electron component. A detailed analysis shows that these mechanisms can significantly influence the electron beam characteristics, leading to a production of high-energy electrons even when the laser beam interacts with a very thick target. A detailed review will now explore the current understanding of these mechanisms and their potential applications, including the development of high-field physics and beam physics.

A platinum foil with a mass of 45.3 grams was utilized in a $0v\beta\beta$ decay search in an ongoing experiment in the CUORICube setup, with the goal of assessing low-level background contamination from radioactive elements like $^{184}$Pt and $^{192}$Pt. A detection device in the CUORICube setup was employed to analyze the $v\beta\beta$ decay of natural platinum isotopes into excited states for 30 days in a position containing the 45.3-gram platinum foil. The obtained limits on double beta decay to excited states are $2\times10^{16}$ (90% confidence level) for the $184$ isotope and $2\times10^{15}$ (90% confidence level) for the $192$ isotope. These limits represent three orders of magnitude improvement over previously documented outcomes for the $184$ isotope and represent the first time these kinds of decay have been looked for in the $192$ isotope. The discovered limits were calculated using a semicircular detector, with a total of 126 kg·km for the $184$ isotope and 72.5 kg·km for the $192$ isotope, which is one of the most sensitive examinations yet conducted.

The value of the renormalization constant $Z_J$ is calculated for a specific dimensional regularization with a particular treatment of the $\gamma_5$ term in QCD with massless quarks to an order of $\alpha_s^3$. The constant's value is determined by evaluating the interactions of the relevant operators within the axial-anomaly equation, where a specific relationship holds between the vacuum, a two-gluon state, and an off-shell gluon. A specific equality is confirmed, showing the equivalence between the renormalization constants for $\alpha_s$ and $Z_{F \tilde{F}}$, a crucial operator involved in the computation. Consequently, a corresponding relationship between their respective anomalous dimensions is confirmed, which follows directly from the validity of the axial-anomaly equation itself. As a result, the relationship between the QCD evolution of $\Delta_{FF}$ and $\alpha_s$ is established.

This study investigates a cutting-edge technique combining images from high dynamic range dual-camera systems to enhance overall image quality. A key benefit of this approach is that it bypasses the limitation of sensor capabilities, thus outperforming single sensors in image processing. A crucial challenge associated with this method lies in aligning images captured under significantly different exposure conditions. To address this issue, a novel deep learning-based approach has been introduced, featuring a exposure estimation module and a patch alignment unit. Through the implementation of a customized patch comparison metric, this model seeks to identify and connect similar image regions across varying exposure levels. A novel weighted patch alignment loss has been introduced to refine image alignment and improve overall image quality. To evaluate its effectiveness, comprehensive experiments were conducted using the real-world MPIUS-Incident dataset and the synthetic MAP1 dataset. To the best knowledge of the researchers, this model represents the first attempt at developing a data-driven solution for exposing and aligning high dynamic range dual-camera images.

Recent studies on the three-dimensional generalized Hamiltonian Ermakov system have been reevaluated and corrected. Contrary to previous claims, we demonstrate that a key finding is erroneous and the classification problem was not thoroughly resolved. By integrating knowledge about the connection between spatial context and movement, we now provide an accurate classification of the three-dimensional system. Our conclusions are further broadened to apply to higher dimensional analogs of the system.

Research in Europe's public transportation reveals that buses are used in around 56% of total journeys. A key factor influencing this figure and broader demand for public transport is service quality. Passengers evaluate quality through various factors such as information accessibility. A proposed approach utilizing data mining and machine learning methodologies to forecast short-term demands for public transport is explored. Specifically, data from GPS sensors and potential factors like weather and time are utilized in a comprehensive model. A case study was conducted in Rome to validate this approach: it involved geographic information systems to determine stop locations and demand prediction, with a focus on GPS data analysis. Sklearn libraries were employed for machine learning algorithms and Map-Reduce techniques used for real-time data processing due to its adaptability. The results showed that incorporating weather data significantly improved the accuracy of demand prediction.

To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011).

We're analyzing systems that have an Adler-Bell-Jackiw anomaly from the perspective of non-invertible symmetry. A unique non-invertible charge defect is introduced, where a crucial factor is a localized current operator on the defect, characterized by continuous elements of a $U(1)$. By leveraging this approach, we establish an extension of Goldstone's theorem for non-invertible symmetries, with a mention of potential applications in string theory.

A semi-transitive graph has no directed cycles and for any sequence of connections, a link is not allowed if it skips over intermediate steps, unless there's a link between the starting and ending points. Unfortunately, checking a graph's semi-transitivity is very computationally demanding. A'split' graph can be broken into two groups - one completely connected and one completely unconnected - with further research conducted on splitting semi-transitive patterns in such graphs. A key finding in this study was proving the non-existence of a particular type of semi-transitive split graph. Building on this discovery, other types of graphs were found to have no semi-transitive split structures either. Additionally, some conclusions were drawn based on natural numbers.

A cutting-edge approach has been developed to accurately identify genuine hadronic tau decays in the CMS detector, distinguishing them from those originating from quarks, gluons, electrons, and muons. By incorporating insights from neighboring particles, this novel method utilizes a sophisticated deep neural network to analyze complex data. As a result, it exhibits marked improvement over its predecessor in discriminating hadronic tau decays, with its performance enhanced by up to 30% (or further) in regions examined. In line with these findings, the CMS experiment has updated its tau identification criteria, incorporating this advanced technique.

Future sky surveys, notably the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), are projected to observe approximately 10 million time-varying celestial sources each night for a decade, sending real-time data streams to brokers for evaluation. Brokers will then utilize machine learning to filter these sources and select the most relevant for various scientific applications. Our investigation explores the merits and complexities of employing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) in classification tasks, especially those requiring event selection. BNNs exhibit high accuracy as classifiers, but our analysis also reveals a significant increase in computation time compared to standard neural networks. Consequently, using BNNs on cloud-based brokers may not be feasible due to their cost. Nevertheless, BNNs show considerable promise for up-to-date classification and event selection for future astronomical survey databases and other challenging classification tasks where computational resources are limited or restrictive.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic crystal fibers, showcasing a substantial conversion efficiency between the HE11 and HE21 modes and reaching a peak gain coefficient of 21.4/W/km. By investigating the impact of fiber parameters, such as microstructured air-hole arrangements and silica-doped core concentrations, we gain insights into their influence on Brillouin gain and serve as guidelines for designing ideal structures. Moreover, we explore the potential applications of this phenomenon for rapid mode coupling control and high-pressure sensing at the nanometer level.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn.

Two modified knapsack models, the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, are two variations of the classic stochastic knapsack problem. These two models usually arise in scenarios such as resource allocation and online advertising. In the general form of the SUKP, the objective is to achieve a set of benefits while adhering to a limited capacity of cost. In the BMCP, the goal is to maximize the coverage of certain elements within a predefined set, constrained by a limited budget. In the BMCP, the cost of selection for each element is not explicitly stated. In this research paper, a parametric approach is utilized to solve the BMCP, using the set-union knapsack problem as a basis for comparison. In the approach, a binary linear programming model is designed to determine the optimal threshold for a given budget, thereby obtaining an exact solution to the BMCP at this threshold. In the results obtained, an analysis of the model's optimality is conducted, followed by a performance evaluation of two solution methods - an exact method using column generation and a greedy algorithm - on random instances of the BMCP. In the experiment, the exact method and the greedy algorithm yield an average relative error of less than 8% and 22.86%, respectively. Churn prevention in business retention is a critical concern, which this research tackles by transforming churn prediction in the online gaming industry into a binary classification task. To address this challenge, the study introduces an algorithm based on recurrent neural networks, which can effectively process the temporal nature of online gaming data. Evaluating model performance, the research utilized machine learning metrics, including accuracy, precision, and recall, and found that specific network architectures excelled in different areas: those with higher precision rates consisting of smaller models with fewer long short term memory neurons, whereas models with higher recall rates had more units and longer memory. Notably, the study found that a fully connected neural network, supported by a convolutional neural network approach, yielded the highest recall of 88.6%, making the former an recommendations for businesses aiming to prevent churn.

We are focusing on the Ising Field Theory, particularly at its scaling limit close to the Curie critical point, when an imaginary external magnetic field is applied. We're thoroughly investigating the Yang-Lee edge singularity within this framework. While the leading edge singularity behavior is primarily determined by the Yang-Lee fixed point, corresponding to minimal Toda deformed Wess-Zumino-Witten theory with $su(2)$, a FAST (free fermions interacting with a soliton) mode contributes to the formation of a logarithmic conjugate pair of the identity field's higher-genus representations in the infrared stable fixed point associated with this critical point, thereby facilitating the merging of the Yang-Lee fixed point with the one resulting from a FAST mode present in the Toda deformed $SU(2)_2$ Wess-Zumino-Witten theory. We are also analyzing the Toda deformed $SU(2)_2$ Wess-Zumino-Witten theory itself, focusing on its representation mode's critical behavior.

Our research shows that lattice calculations can be used to derive transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions, with gluons, through large-calculations in lattice regularization. We find that, as calculated in three, four and five dimensions, gluonic TMDPDFs exhibit regularization dependence while evolving towards a regularization-independent state at a specific momentum scale. The findings highlight the capability of gluonic TMDPDFs calculated in various dimensions for use in quasi-PDF analysis. The research suggests that, in order to be consistent with perturbative predictions, a specific mathematical procedure should be applied. The findings highlight the capability of gluonic TMDPDFs calculated in various dimensions for use in quasi-PDF analysis. In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through a process called photon-photon fusion, resulting in a broad range of lepton creation in space around the collision point. Those electron-positron pairs formed near heavy nuclei are then subject to strong interactions. Researchers have used the b-space EPA model to calculate the spatial distribution of positrons and negative electrons generated in such interactions. The findings show that an impressive number of lepton pairs can be produced in a wide range, and these lepton pairs are often positioned close to heavy nuclei. Furthermore, open questions surrounding these lepton production rates and spatial distributions have been raised. The research has significant implications for studying photon interactions in cosmic events and laboratory experiments, particularly in understanding cosmic neutrinos and potential new physics. The research also has implications for other processes, such as photon production and the production of hadrons, when particle trajectories are traced based on the b-space EPA model in further study.

To minimize pollution, bicycle usage is experiencing a resurgence, particularly in urban environments. Despite the trend towards decreased fatalities in other traffic groups, the opposite holds true for cyclists. Therefore, tracking cyclist data is essential to improving their safety by providing city planners with data to plan and construct more cyclist-friendly roads. This study proposes a comprehensive, visually-driven approach to evaluate route risk levels. This method uses a combination of GPS data, visual features, and image-based processing to enhance precision. By using a graph-based algorithm to connect GPS points with road images, the route can be fully visualized. This route is then segmented into sections based on road type to serve as a key factor in risk assessment. To assess visual risk, a CNN model with a tri-partite attention mechanism is proposed, able to extract relevant features from images while considering the importance of GPS data and road type class information. This method's efficacy is demonstrated through its development to estimate route risk levels using a dataset of stricken cyclists in the US. Following thorough testing, the proposed approach shows significant improvement over baseline risk assessment methods, with AUC scores increasing by nearly 5%. All code for this method can be accessed on a public repository.

A novel method using the RRT algorithm is introduced to create a safety-critical path by enforcing Control Barrier Functions and robot kinodynamic constraints while minimizing computation. The path planning problem is reformulated with constraints from Control Barrier Functions and robot kinodynamics, represented through a mixed-integer quadratic program. The strategy involves periodically sampling the MBMPQ, and using a RRT* algorithm modified with a heuristic, to generate a sequence of candidate paths. A filter process is applied to eliminate samples that violate the constraints, and a quadratic optimization is performed with the constrained samples to yield a near-optimal, safe path. The modification of the RRT* algorithm allows it to generate on-the-fly feasible sub-paths, and the introduction of the heuristic facilitates search direction and reduces search time. Experimental results demonstrate the RRT* algorithm can generate paths similar to RRT* with the heuristic in half the time, and the approach is shown to be effective in mobile robots and spacecraft simulation.

The smallest possible size of such a cover for $R$ is referred to as the covering number $\sigma(R)$ of $R$,
and if $\sigma(R)$ is less than the covering number of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is considered $\sigma$-elementary.
For rings with a unity, the size of a cover of $R$ is limited by the size of a maximal right ideal of $R$,
so if $\sigma(R)$ is less than the size of a maximal right ideal of a quotient ring $R/I$, $R$ is known as $\sigma$-elementary.

Recent investigations have highlighted deep neural networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs. However, existing countermeasures are largely insufficient. In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain and restrict the impact of malicious inputs. Additionally, by equating deep neural networks with neural ODEs, we demonstrate that a neural network's inherent properties also confer its deep ODE equivalent with a certain level of robustness against adversarial examples. Importantly, this robustness stems from the inherent characteristics of ODEs, thus eliminating the need for any ad hoc solutions or rely on specific dataset properties. Moreover, our research reveals that a neural network's direct transformation into a differential equation offers a unified explanation for both its natural robustness and its ability to generalize across various datasets. Furthermore, based on our analysis, we develop a range of robust training methods that can be applied to both neural networks and their deep ODE equivalents. Experimental results have demonstrated the efficacy of these methods.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the convolution of a given kernel and a solution, extensively applied to model vehicular traffic, have a singular local limit that has been extensively studied. This singular limit is about nonlocal solutions converging to the entropy-admissible solution of a classical conservation law with a point source, this point source being the convolution kernel. In traffic modeling, this singular local limit yields the well-known Lighthill-Whitham traffic flow model. In this paper, we explore the well-posedness of the nonlocal conservation laws with a convolution-based flux under a pointsource assumption, and show that under this condition the solutions converge to the classical Lighthill-Whitham traffic flow model. Furthermore, in traffic modeling, we find that nonlocal solutions converge to the classical model even when the kernel contains a pointsource component, with the convergence result remaining valid for the well-posed solution, hence even for the solutions that do not converge to the classical model. In addition to that, in traffic modeling, we find that nonlocal solutions converge to the classical model if the kernel is bounded above a certain value, with the convergence result remaining valid for the models that do not contain a pointsource, hence even for the models that do not have a classical limit. Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow transition maps to be multiplied by a scalar greater than one, while still maintaining a homeomorphism. Research has revealed that dilation surfaces with a homeomorphism that falls within a range between one and two are generally structurally similar. However, the current knowledge on surfaces with a homeomorphism that exceeds two is limited. Recent breakthroughs have identified that certain compact dilation surfaces do exist with a homeomorphism that exceeds two, and we have further established that these surfaces can be comprised of a single component or be comprised of multiple surfaces connected by loops and must possess a sufficiently high number of intersections.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions as a more comprehensive alternative to conventional pair-wise measures such as correlation and mutual information. Building on this concept, we developed a whole brain connectivity network based on total correlation and demonstrated its potential to serve as a biomarker for brain alterations. Specifically, we employed Correlation Explanation to estimate total correlation in a fMRI dataset of 73 Alzheimer's patients downloaded from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and showed that through network analysis of this metric, we can distinguish between different stages of the disease. Moreover, we found that certain regions of the brain exhibit distinct patterns of total correlation changes across different stages of the disease.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory is adapted to represent the non-linear 
Moyal deformation of canonical commutation relations in the complex phase 
space. This is achieved by combining Hilbert-space direct decompositions into 
smooth wave functions and complex coordinate functions. Our first key 
observation is that this process mirrors the wave-particle duality from quantum 
mechanics. We extend the established methods to unitary representations of 
finite-dimensional Lie groups within the Moyal phase space. This work draws 
inspiration from Bergmann's work on the complex Story of a small world system.

As the scope of Gaussian processes widens, the availability of simple mathematical solutions dwindles, prompting the need for alternative methods. Monte Carlo simulations serve as an intermediary between complicated mathematical formulas and applicable predictions by randomly sampling a variable and using it as a rough estimate. Traditionally, this is done through deterministic methods which derive a deterministic approximation based on random data and then utilize it to generate new samples. However, these methods fall short for Gaussian processes as they fail to account for the uncertainty in the mathematical model. To overcome this limitation, probabilistic methods are used by first creating a probability distribution based on random data and then utilizing it to generate new samples. A major advantage of these methods is that they can leverage the power of graphics processing units to speed up the sampling process, but their efficiency decreases with the size and complexity of the data. A new, hierarchical probability bin approach is presented for Gaussian processes, achieving faster computation and a reduced memory requirement of up to thirty times less compared to other methods for the same level of accuracy.

This research demonstrates that in outdoor settings with wireless communications employing the IEEE 802.11 protocol using dipole antennas, ground reflection is a dominant signal reflection. We've developed a mathematical model to determine the phase difference between the direct signal and the ground-reflected signal. We've also conducted an experiment to verify this model's accuracy, and obtained similar results for different transmitter and receiver positions. This ground-reflected signal has potential uses in fingerprint-based localization techniques.

The last ten years have been marked by significant breakthroughs in neutrino physics. Notably, multiple studies have confirmed the existence of neutrino oscillations caused by neutrino flavor state mixing. Key constraints on neutrino properties were placed, and the first direct observation of neutrino interactions was made, which came in the form of a spectral distortion in the energy distribution of surviving neutrinos after interaction. Moreover, the presence of CP violation in neutrino interactions was constrained using existing experiments. We present the primary outcomes of the most important neutrino experiments from this ten-year period.

Research on top tagging has advanced due to the top quark's prominence in studying physics that goes beyond the standard model. Recent studies have found that machine learning techniques can improve in probing new physics at the Low-Energy Electron-Positron Collider. This can be achieved by applying these methods to the semi-leptonic channel at the collider. Researchers have identified that several signatures of new physics can be represented as overlapping sets of observables. This has enabled them to develop a systematic top tagging scheme based on the observables from the t \bar t j events and a sole variable for the 4 fermion final states. This has also resulted in a comparable performance when the model parameters are adjusted to accommodate beyond standard model scenarios.
