Our non-resonant associated production calculations also reveal considerable detectability limits for vector-like quark partners, especially when produced singly with small couplings to Gluons, which might explain the lack of observed new physics so far.

A recent breakthrough in translating English to SPARQL using neural machine translation (NMT) models holds great promise for all-around query support, but these models still struggle to generate complex queries effectively. To improve this limitation, we introduce a innovative approach that combines knowledge graphs to augment the training data for a more well-rounded translation performance. This method, called kg-TTT, not only boosts the quality of translations but also increases accuracy by up to 84.1% in query accuracy without any further refinement.

This work introduces a novel method for systematically categorizing and assessing the quality of diverse publishing outlets in Computer Science. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. By treating authorship patterns at individual publishing venues as a predictive task and focusing on key performance metrics, our method generates high-accuracy quality scores for every recorded conference and journal. Furthermore, our scores can also be utilized to model and track shifts in field dynamics across different periods. In addition, our scores can serve as a basis for evaluating both individual researchers and academic institutions, demonstrating quantitative evaluations comparable to those derived from citation analysis or peer review processes. In contrast to many prevailing evaluation methods, our solution's reliance on extensive, publicly accessible data enables seamless replication and validation. In a collaborative spirit, our complete code and dataset have been shared publicly at https://github.com/leonidk/venue_scores for the purpose of facilitating further development upon this research.

Advanced learning methods can address longstanding control challenges, but the complex neural networks used pose significant analysis difficulties regarding the safety of control systems. Fortunately, recent research has introduced methods for analyzing and verifying the complex control systems. This tutorial synthesizes and introduces techniques for verifying the robustness of neural networks that originated in related fields. These techniques are further applied to establish guarantees for systems that combine a neural network and a control system. Ultimately, these tools facilitate the analysis of safe control systems and provide rigorous verification for control designers.

This study builds upon three significant lines of research related to dissimilarity-based clustering and integrates them into a unified framework that provides a principle-driven approach to clustering. Specifically, it draws from Jardine and Sibson's concept of overlapping clusters, Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's functorial approach to partition-based clustering, and the notion of unstable homotopy groups of difficulty in Blanca et al.'s work on the topological clustering of dense sets. Carlsson and M\'{e}moli's work emphasizes the importance of qualitative attributes, whereas the other two sources stress the role of distances in the clustering process. By extending the results of Blanca et al. to any dissimilarity space, even those that are not metric, we are able to generalize the concepts of difficulty and stable clustering at the level of the homotopy group. This allows us to provide the first proof that the stable n-th homotopy group of difficulty provides a clustering scheme for n-point sets that are linearly separable.

Tensor completion techniques seek to recover incomplete data in observed tensors by leveraging their low-rank properties, particularly useful in applications like video and multidimensional data recovery. However, when dealing with incremental data such as streaming videos, it's crucial to maintain balance between recovering low-rank data and handling increasing amounts of incipient data. Existing methods either heavily prioritize low-rank data recovery or accommodate growing incipient data, but often neglect the other aspect. This research presents a new tensor completion method, developed using semidefinite programming, that effectively recovers low-rank data while dynamically adjusting to changing incipient data on a per-step basis without storing past data. Moreover, it's the first method to handle incremental data in a way that simultaneously minimizes errors and maintains low-rank properties in completed tensors. To evaluate this method, a benchmark dataset was developed from YouTube videos and experiment results show the method's ability to successfully complete tensors from incrementing videos while recovering low-rank data up to three dimensions.

It is demonstrated that except in three specific instances, the conjugacy classes of classical Weyl groups $W(B_{n})$ and $W(D_{n})$ take the form of type D. This finding has implications for the Nichols algebras associated with irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules over the classical Weyl groups $\mathbb W_{n}$, revealing that these algebras have infinite dimensions, with the exception of three distinct cases: the $(2, 3),(1^{2}, 3)$ case in $\mathbb S_{4}$, and the $(1^{n-2}, 2)$ case in $\mathbb S_{n}$ for $n >4$.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic and intermittent, downscale energy transport. In the recent past, researchers have successfully isolated and characterized an equilibrium wave-turbulence state within rotating systems, marked by a scenario involving an imbalance of momentum and energy distribution among different vortices. In a recent study, researchers have provided mathematical proof that downscale energy transport in rotating systems in a state of equilibrium is facilitated by two interacting and move asymmetric wave-turbulence components, one characterized by two-dimensional and the other by three-dimensional vortices. In this work, researchers have provided the first experimental description of the role played by three-dimensional geostrophic vortices in facilitating energy transport in rotating systems in a state of equilibrium. Our findings within rotating systems in a state of equilibrium reveal a significantly different mechanism of energy transport in comparison to that observed in another phenomenon, which is believed to be influenced by the combination of inertia and vorticity.

We investigate a basic model called Iterative Graph Normalization (IGN) for analyzing weighted graphs. The model employs a local transformation applied to adjacent edge weights, followed by repeated iterations. A key aspect is to identify the most effective sequence of edge weight updates using the current graph configuration. Although this problem is complex given the vast number of possible edge configurations, we prove that IGN's optimal solution relies on a specific set of key graph properties. As a result, we can limit our search to a manageable set of properties for the first time. We discuss two suitable optimization strategies to narrow down the solution space even further. In the first strategy, we directly identify the optimal set of graph properties, and in the second, we use a local search procedure to iteratively refine the solution. In the second case, we show that each local search step yields a better or at least equally good solution compared to the previous one. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on how much the graph's overall weight can be reduced through IGN. The model presents several useful properties, such as: (a) each iterative step doesn't increase the (maximal) clique sizes of the graph; (b) IGN doesn't remove minimal weighted edges from maximal cliques; and (c) it can be viewed as a form of 2x independent set extractor with a good probability of success. To further investigate the efficacy of IGN, we tested the approach on five popular benchmark graph collections and found the resulting normalized graphs to be significantly

This research studies the impact of a magnetic field and electron mobility on electrically modulated single-layer graphene, in contrast to a conventional two-dimensional electron gas system. The unique structure of electrically modulated graphene, featuring two non-interacting bands, one of which is completely filled, results in intriguing thermodynamic properties that differ significantly from those of a 2DEG system. Due to the absence of a mobility edge in electrically modulated graphene, even minor changes in electron temperature can cause a substantial transfer of carriers from the filled to the unfilled band. This transfer is heavily influenced by a magnetic field, leading to a landau level-dependent structure in carrier distribution. Consequently, unique thermodynamic properties emerge, such as a temperature-dependent specific heat and a non-linear variation in electrical resistivity in response to temperature changes. Our findings provide valuable insights that can guide the design of electrically modulated graphene for innovative device applications.

Recent findings have identified low-frequency radio emission from systems consisting of small cool stars called M dwarfs, which shares similar patterns to magnetospheric phenomena observed in our Solar System. The radio emission could be driven by a star-planet interaction or an unstable balance in a rotating disk and the surrounding stellar magnetic field. A new monitoring campaign observed the M dwarf system CR Draconis, consisting of multiple observing sessions taken over a period of approximately two years, which resulted in a substantial total on-source time of around six days. The study found that CR Draconis emits radio signal 90 percent of the time with low frequency and has a specific circular polarization pattern. A low-frequency radio signal and circular polarization were detected multiple times, which matched the expected characteristics of an language neutral wind that balances the disk and the star's magnetic field. A pulse of high-frequency radiation, specifically 2.85 GHz, was detected in one occasion, which could be caused by a star-planet interaction or an explosion on the star. The study found that the star's magnetic field could be at a specific value and that the detected radio signals could be seen multiple times based on that assumption. A low-frequency radio signal, specifically 16.7 MHz, was detected two occasions and could be seen multiple times based on that model.

By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations, which can otherwise impair the neural network's
performance. In our new approach, Articulated Neural Rendering (ARnR), we use a
mesh-agnostic system to learn the articulation-independent appearance of a mesh
and decouple it from the articulation-dependent appearance. We successfully apply
this method to various skinned mesh datasets for realistic rendering of virtual human
avatars under changing lighting. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate substantial
improvements, specifically in terms of visual quality and computational efficiency,
when comparing ArnR to traditional three-dimensional surface reconstruction and
neural volume rendering methods for rendering animated characters.

Recent advances in artificial neural networks (ANNs) claim to simulate advanced animal cognition, including human vision. Researchers investigated whether six state-of-the-art networks, ranging from single to multilayer architectures, could match human efficiency and human-like mistakes on an array of image processing tasks. The tasks included identifying objects, recognizing scenes, and interpreting contexts, all of which were drawn from the ImageNet database with a high level of detail. The evaluation revealed that the ANNs excelled in object recognition but fell short on more complex scene and context understanding tasks, particularly under degraded image conditions. The ANNs' performance deficits aligned with those observed in existing psychological research, suggesting that animal cognition studies could inform both computational vision and psychological science. The results also underscored the importance of carefully evaluating computer vision models on a broader range of tasks than just object recognition.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and a specific link in a specific context of Chern-Simons theory is examined in this study. Specifically, we demonstrate how the AW algebra's generators correlate with the Chern-Simons theory's coupling constant and the winding number, with each generating an invariant under changes in either variable. Furthermore, we establish that the algebra's Casimir element matches the Chern-Simons theory's generation of the link invariant when expressed in terms of a specific algebraic function.

Our study presents computational findings based on a novel trimer-cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulation approach, which enables the exploration of two- and three-dimensional complex lattice structures in an exact manner. We examine the thermodynamic properties of an unstable distorted kagome lattice model and present the specific heat, which exhibits a two-peak structure, in addition to evaluating the ground state energy and the spin susceptibility for a frustrated, two-dimensional Brillouin magnetic system in the vicinity of its quantum critical point.

Pre-trained language models, exemplified by GPT-3, have exhibited an unexpected capacity for zero-shot learning. Specifically, to accomplish this, it is possible to utilize a limited number of "seed" sentences to generate a table of conditional probabilities. These probabilities can then serve as a form of "quality score" to filter a vast database of possible sentences, ultimately allowing for various tasks like text generation, translation, or summarization. Moreover, recent research has demonstrated that with sufficient computational resources, it is feasible to optimize these conditional probabilities through an iterative process: maximizing the likelihood of the desired output given the input. This optimized probability can in turn be used as a quality metric for zero-shot learning. However, it is essential to minimize the space requirements associated with storing the conditional probability table. To address this, we have proposed a novel technique – meta-tuning – to obtain a condensed representation of the conditional probability table. This is achieved by expressing the original probabilities as a linear combination of a limited number of basic "meta-states". The weights for this linear combination can then be learned via a gradient-based optimization process. As a result, the space requirements associated with storing the conditional probability table can be significantly reduced. Additionally, we have found that this compressed representation can facilitate efficient communication, for example, when loading the model onto a GPU.

In depth research into the likelihood and characteristics of a strong first-order electroweak phase transition has been carried out as a prerequisite to studying electroweak baryogenesis within the context of the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM, considering recent data from the Higgs sector, dark matter searches, and analyses from the Large Hadron Collider involving lighter charginos and neutralinos. This includes thorough reviews of the latest relevant LHC studies. Several generic model scans under constraints from the Higgs mass distribution, dark matter observations, and LHC data have been conducted to gather insights into parameter relationships, and these results have been presented in various projection scans. However, it has become apparent that several of these results necessitate a more in-depth examination beyond the plane of the $Z_3$ invariant $s$-conjugate singlet Higgs sector to better comprehend complex interactions between the two sectors involved. Consequently, two illustrative case studies have been created utilizing two-point functions derived from the $Z_3$-invariant potential to gain a deeper and more refined understanding of the landscape. These refined analyses have enabled the determination of likelihoods for the occurrence of a strong first-order phase transition under various conditions, and they have revealed that several of these regions remain inaccessible to current LHC studies.

We introduce novel approaches for visually identifying reliable redshifts through emission lines in the millimeter and submillimeter spectrum. Our methodology involves evaluating the effectiveness of diverse millimeter and submillimeter emission lines in different redshift ranges, accounting for noise in spectroscopic data, and navigating potential contamination from optical and UV lines. To facilitate this process, we provide data to compute the autocorrelation function of galaxy spectra and a metric to assess signal versus noise in pairs of millimeter and submillimeter emission lines. Our work includes a comprehensive catalog of robust redshift indicators across redshift values from 0 to 15. We also simulate a model to estimate the redshift distribution of millimeter and submillimeter galaxies with known redshift values, demonstrating its usefulness in the context of the CosmoSim galaxy catalog. However, even with these robust redshift indicators, achieving high confidence in redshift identifications often requires a trade-off between the presence of detectable emission lines and desired measurement uncertainties.

This research uses large-scale matrix-product state simulations to determine the dynamical spin structure factor of the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a square lattice with antiferromagnetic properties. A highly complex phase diagram arises from the lattice symmetry and spin symmetry. The researchers focus their efforts on the $J_2/(J_1+J_2)$ ratio in the regions of high and low $J_1$ values. In the high $J_1$ value region, the spin system exhibits a 120-degree-ordered phase with two distinct interrelated quasiparticle branches, the long and short wave number branch being a proof of fermi physics and middle energy branch being a signature of $J_2$ induced effect. A different behavior is observed in the low $J_1$ value region where the spin system displays two distinct phases, the liquid and nematic phase, with two distinct interrelated quasiparticle branches once again being observed but this time with an emphasis on nematic structure and an almost complete suppression of the long wave number branch.

The study explores lattice cutoff effects on the phase transition in SU(3) Higgs theory across four dimensions, with a varying number of lattice sites in the spatial and temporal dimensions, using bare complex three-doublet Higgs fields. The investigation reveals that the phase transition becomes smoother as the volume increases, especially with two and three temporal sites, but retains a discontinuity with six temporal sites. Cutoff effects are analyzed through various parameters and a comparison with electroweak physics at all orders of perturbation theory reveals that the lattice model shares certain characteristics with its continuum counterpart, such as a non-zero critical Higgs field value and a specific critical temperature. Furthermore, the study finds that the phase transition is influenced by a suppression factor affecting the Higgs field and a ratio of critical temperatures from the lattice and electroweak models, which varies significantly based on the number of temporal sites.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a tetragonal structure with P4/mmm symmetry and is predicted to be a nearly ideal two-dimensional ferromagnet. However, its magnetism has yet to be experimentally confirmed. We report on the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al using a range of techniques, including resistance, magnetization, and muon spin relaxation experiments, where a N\'{e}el temperature of $T_N$ = 125 K was determined through magnetometry and muon spin relaxation, with a ferrimagnetic ordering at 2 K as observed in all measurements. The established $T_N$ value closely aligns with theoretical predictions and is accompanied by a Curie-Weiss behavior below 200 K. Moreover, it was found that magnetizing the sample leads to significant changes in its crystal structure, with magnetometry indicating a COE of 2.3 meV and an IME of 1.3 meV. The experimentally determined parameters align with theoretical predictions for a 2D ferromagnet. Additionally, muon K-resistance measurements reveal a a parameter of 0.67 meV $\mu_0$. As a two-dimensional system, Cr$_2$Al displays a unique low-field susceptibility of 420 $\mu$emcu, with a depth of 1000 $\mu$emcu indicating a two-dimensional nature. The experimentally found ferrimagnetic ordering and $q$-dependent spin ordering align with theoretical

A new kinetic model, the $
u$-model, is developed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $
u$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating the inherent characteristics of gas particle collisions. Established models like the Buckley model are found to be restrictive as they assume identical collision frequencies for various velocities, thereby failing to account for velocity gradients in polyatomic gases. In contrast, the $
u$-model's velocity-dependent collision frequency facilitates a seamless transition from established equations, while providing an analytical expression for a monatomic gas in an equilibrium state. Subsequently, the $
u$-model is applied to strengthen the strengths of established kinetic models, thereby allowing for the accurate simulation of rarefied monatomic and polyatomic gas flows. In a crucial departure from established models, the $
u$-model is analyzed in a non-equilibrium state, thereby offering a simplified yet robust approach for polyatomic gas simulations.

Voice assistant applications, such as Alexa and Google Assistant, significantly
benefit from advancements in semantic parsing, a core challenge in NLP. The
traditional approach to semantic parsing relies on abundant labeled data, a
resource scarce and costly to annotate. In this research, we present a new
groundbreaking method called Low Rank Multi-relation Assignment Parsing (LMAP),
designed to tackle the challenge without labeled data. The proposed technique
involves generating multiple hierarchical assignments between concepts and their
connections, followed by a common parsing interpretation. This is achieved by
constrained optimization of a model, breaking down into manageable components
utilizing the Dual Decomposition strategy. We assessed LMAP on both key entity and
relation recognition tasks using the standard Benchmarks dataset. The results
 demonstrate LMAP's potential to produce accurate output given only unlabelled
data, a significant advancement.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. To determine crucial information, precise measurements of heavy quarks formed at these high-energy interactions are vital. To obtain this information, researchers will employ cutting-edge heavy flavor detectors offering enhanced sensitivity, specifically in understanding the distribution of quarks within protons and nuclei. Additionally, advancements in open and closed heavy flavor hadron, heavy jet, and heavy fragment measurements will offer valuable insights into the creation and evolution of quarks and gluons, ultimately contributing to advancements in theoretical models and practical tools for simulating these complex interactions.

A new discovery in X-ray variability patterns in four galaxies, identified as Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs) and two Quasi-Periodic Oscillations (QPOs), suggests the use of Fourier transforms can distinguish these phenomena from other variable patterns. However, the QPEs region of the Fourier diagram includes a wide range of frequencies, resembling a "butterfly" shape, and can contain noise or strong peaks, making it harder to distinguish from other patterns. To better understand these variables, a new approach using Gaussian processes in the Repeatedly variable patterns in the amplitude and frequency fields (RAPAF) method has been developed. The RAPAF method creates separate models for the amplitude and frequency of variable patterns and can better distinguish between QPEs and QPOs in the Fourier diagrams, especially in identifying the multi-component nature of QPEs and separating noise from QPEs and QPOs. Additionally, the RAPAF method can reveal patterns in the time series data that are not apparent in other diagrams, such as multiple peaks in the light curves in 4U1543-437, and can confirm previous findings in other sources, such as the cyclotron line in GX 1631-423.

The existence of magnetic fields in stars has long sparked debate about their influence on the atmospheres of stars. Recent findings from the SPIRou instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope have provided insights into the properties of magnetic fields in early-type main sequence stars. We report on SPIRur's capabilities to study these fields and present observations of two early-type main sequence stars with significant magnetic fields. We observed the stellar magnetic fields using SPIRou's polarimetric mode and discovered that the magnetic fields in these stars weaken significantly in their upper atmospheres. Our data indicate a decline of approximately $10^3$ Gauss in magnetic field strength at greater than 1.2 stellar radii from the center. We report for the first time observations of the variability in magnetic fields in these stars over short periods of time and find a high probability for variability in the magnetic fields of these specific stars to change within a 2-hour period. Our findings are consistent with the magnetic fields in these stars being shaped by the cumulative effects of flares and coronal mass ejections.

A link exists between a Dunkl operator over a field with two elements and a first derivative, 
exemplified through its equivalence to an operator set representing one-dimensional oscillator motion.
This equivalence holds in that the operator translates the classical Hermite polynomials into the generalized Hermite polynomials.

We demonstrate that two continuous minimal actions of the infinite dihedral group on an infinite compact Hausdorff space can be orbit equivalent if and only if they are conjugate, provided the group in question remains unchanged. However, this equivalency breaks down when considering other virtually cyclic groups like the direct product of the integer group and a non-abelian finite simple group, especially when these are used instead of the infinite dihedral group.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(X) | \mathcal{A_x}]$, where $X$ is a non-compact, zero-mean, and $\mathcal{F}$-valued Gaussian random variable. The operator $P$ is used to describe its functional behavior. Given that calculating the exact operator $(P - \lambda_i)^{-1}$ is computationally expensive, we explore the feasibility of approximating this operator with a Hilbert--Schmidt perturbation, which can be more efficiently calculated. Our study provides a new perspective on the perturbation by showing that its error term is logarithmically dependent on the inverse perturbation size and the resulting approximate operator has a finite Hilbert--Schmidt norm. Furthermore, we verify the effectiveness of this perturbation in a variety of $L^2$-approximations and offer a straightforward way of obtaining smoother representations of the operator $(P - \lambda_i)^{-1}$. Additionally, we outline the broader applicability of this approach in approximating operators associated with Markov chain Gibbs measures.

Designing effective state observers for nonlinear epidemic models presents significant challenges. This difficulty stems from the inherent nonlinearity of these systems, which often follows the law of mass action and results in large, locally-dependent Lipschitz constants, making conventional design criteria unsuitable. This paper introduces a new state observer that improves estimation capabilities for nonlinear systems, including epidemic models, by mitigating the influence of nonlinearity in the error system dynamics. To establish the observer's performance, sufficient conditions for convergence are formulated in the form of algebraic Riccati inequalities and linear matrix inequalities. These conditions provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing the observer's design for accurate state estimation.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in downstream applications as well. Although numerous KE models exist, there is currently a lack of clear guidance on selecting which temporal models to combine, and what weight to assign them, for optimal results. This paper introduces a novel ensemble method called TempOral Guide to Plugging in Effective Relations (TOPR) that addresses this issue. By using a network to determine relationships between temporal embeddings and their contributions to overall performance, and weighing them effectively, TOPR is able to achieve superior results on tasks such as link prediction and question answering, and outperform many existing KE models. Top results are available at https://github.com/wangtynn/TOPR.

Research driven by ultrashort pulses from Kerr-lens mode-locked oscillators has spawned significant advancement in numerous fields. To tackle the limitations of high-power applications, an extension of this theory, known as the "kinetic method", can predict the geometry of pulse-shaping devices like ring resonators in high-power scenarios. We propose a revision to the kinetic method by incorporating non-Kerr effects into the analysis. By applying this approach to the specific case of a twin-tiya mode-killer inside an optical pulse shaper, we gain insight into its ability to prevent temporal solitons. Our prediction matches well with simulations from the well-established beam propagation method. Furthermore, it offers understanding of its performance without the need for the usually intensive three-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

Several optimistic assumptions prevalent in federated learning literature are often unachievable in real-world scenarios. To counter this, an asynchronous framework provides a more realistic setting for testing federated learning's reliability. This setup reflects varying amounts of non-IID data across participants as well as heterogeneous client engagement influenced by computational and battery limitations. Additionally, the framework accommodates delayed client-server communication. To alleviate the high communication overhead associated with asynchronous online federated learning (ASO-Fed), we employed partial data sharing, which minimizes participants' communication loads and makes participating in the learning process more manageable. Notably, we proved the ASO-Fed model with partial data sharing converges, enabled by this proof, we provide the first evidence that online federated learning can succeed in realistic, asynchronous settings, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach through a range of experiments.

To improve the efficiency of thin-film silicon solar cells with limited light absorption, researchers investigate a back reflector with a nanostructured 3D photonic band gap crystal made from silicon that can easily be integrated into the existing thin films.  Using computational methods, the team calculates the optical properties of the crystal by solving Maxwell's equations, showing that it can significantly enhance absorption within the cells by offering a tailored scattering effect.  By achieving this, the band gap crystal increases the energy absorbed from the sun and reduces dependence on thin films with enhanced absorption depths.  For a given thickness of 501 nm, introducing a photonic crystal with a 63.5 vol% occupied by silicon yields an absorption increase of 39.5%, mainly through diffuse reflector scattering; this contrasts with a standard metal back almirage that offers 84.3 vol% silicon absorption.  Moreover, this increased absorption occurs while maintaining high diffuse reflectivity at the back surface of the film, ensuring both radiative and irradiance enhancements.  An alternative design involving a simpler 2D photonic crystal made from silicon, applied on top of an existing thin silicon film, also shows scattering effects and improved absorption by 19.5% compared to the existing standard metal back surface when covering a 501 nm thick thin film.

We have derived a set of holomorphic functions, denoted by $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$, which, when the absolute value of $s$ tends to infinity in the right half-plane, behave similarly to iterated exponentials. The functions are of interest in relation to $\lambda$-booms and $\mu$-crashes as seen in nested root systems, and their properties are influenced by the parameters $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Building on previous work by Borovoi and Van der Kallen, we have found that $\mu$ can be expressed as an iterated exponentiation of $\pm 1$, depending on the sign of $\lambda$. When $\lambda$ is nonnegative, we have proven that $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$ represents the Newtonian degree of a certain algebraic group homomorphism. This result generalizes a previous finding by Borovoi and Van der Kallen, specifically for $\mu = \pm 1$. In addition, we have determined the Newtonian degree of certain homomorphisms in types $A_{2n-3}$, $D_{2n-3}$, and $D_{2n-2}$. We have also found a connection between the functions $\beta_{\lambda,\mu} (s)$ and the Newton-Newton degree of $Sp_{2n} (\mathbb{C})$ through the application of Weyl and Newton's

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first discovered high dimensional expanders.

Incorporating Black Box Robertson-Serre rigidity theorems enabled us to sparsify links without compromising the infinite dimensional nature of the constructed Y. Our research also marks a first in providing a constructive, rather than a randomized, construction of a high dimensional expander, along with a significant area of application in showing that there exist infinite simplicial complexes with a small cover of a specific property regarding rank one loops.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach using X-ray diffraction, inelastic neutron scattering, and muon spin relaxation techniques. The results showed that the compound exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior at temperatures of 1.3 K (\(T_{\mathbf{M1}}\)) and 1.7 K (\(T_{\mathbf{M2}}\)), validating predictions from density functional theory. The experimentally determined magnetic moment at the iron-like 5f orbital matched the calculated value, indicating that the Delocalization of this electron state is minimal. The momentum-dependent and temperature-dependent analysis of the inelastic neutron scattering data revealed a strong correlation between the energy and temperature, which could be modeled using a power-law with an exponential dependence. The observed exponential temperature dependence may be attributed to the presence of magnetic impurities or defects. The muon spin relaxation rate showed a logarithmic temperature dependence and initially increased slowly with muon implantation depth, peaking at about 20 ns around 30 Kelvin, from which the hybridization width was estimated at 65 meV. The limited hybridization of the 5f electron state was also confirmed by the muon spin relaxation rate. The measured macroscopic Curie temperature was found to be 1.53 K. The compound exhibits isotropic magnetic properties below its critical temperature and acts as a typical Kondo-lattice antiferromagnet

The application of graph embedding for predicting links in complex networks has shown remarkable success, but most real-world networks are sparse, which are currently underserved by this field. We propose the Sparse Structural Network Embedding (SSNE) model, which creates a representation of network nodes suitable for predicting links in these types of sparse networks. Initially, our model converts the network's adjacency matrix into a Sum of local Neighborhoods (SON) matrix by grouping close elements of the matrix together. By utilizing the SON matrix, our SSNE framework further refines the embedding of nodes through a dynamic partitioning approach that adapts to the network's natural grouping of elements. Our comprehensive experiments on seven sparse networks demonstrate that SSNE consistently surpasses existing graph embedding models, and we showcase its practical applications by utilizing the learned embeddings to predict links, reduce the cost of advertising on Redditan alternative platform, discover has more relevant items and bring up contextual more accurate recommendations on a dataset of mobile app installations.

A low-cost water jet process is employed to achieve a 6mm deep silicon etch, overcoming depth limitations and enabling the creation of a deep atomic vapor cell. Although initial vapor cell designs had a shallower etch of 2.3mm, further refinement using a heat treatment and fine-tuned gas mixture overcame depth constraints. The 6mm deep silicon etch enables the optimization of vapor cell dimensions to minimize systematic errors in frequency shifts, enhancing the performance of laser-driven cold atom research. Furthermore, this work showcases the conversion of a conventional 3mm silicon etch into a deep vapor cell, offering a reliable manufacturing approach for various applications.

We evaluate the precision of a recently proposed nonlinear interference model for a wide range of dual-polarization 4D formats, exhibiting an average disparity with split-step Fourier simulations of no more than 0.1 dB.

Preemptive wildfire detection is critical for minimizing ecological harm, property damage, and human loss. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although DL-based image fusion techniques have been widely applied across various fields, their use in detecting fires from static images is still a relatively new area of research. In this research paper, we present an innovative multi-model fusion approach for wildfire detection using Visible and Infrared images taken simultaneously. Our proposed methodology incorporates multiple features extracted from V-I datasets using state-of-the-art DL architectures. Performance evaluation of multi-model and ensemble strategies on four prominent V-I wildfire detection models verified our hypothesis, yielding a 4% improvement in $\mathcal{A}$ metric and a 23% reduction in error rate, thereby supporting their use as robust multi-feature fusion strategies. These findings show that using pre-trained DL models can speed up the development process of wildfire detection applications using V-I images. Moreover, the integration of diverse features extracted from images using algorithms can significantly enhance the accuracy of wildfire detection.

Early detection and treatment of depression is essential to prevent severe repercussions, making the utilization of multiple detection methods necessary, particularly when they do not rely on physical examinations.  Observing social media expression patterns is highly advantageous for identifying mental health, since individuals tend to express their emotions openly on these platforms.  While current systems utilize social media data to diagnose mental health, they typically struggle with depression, a condition characterized by a lower frequency of social media posts.  Therefore, this study aims to address this issue by developing a framework that enables depression detection at three levels - mild, moderate, and severe - using a dataset derived from social media posts.  The framework employs two techniques, vertical and horizontal splitting, to ensure that social media data is evenly distributed among learners.  The proposed method has demonstrated superior performance compared to baseline approaches in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score on the constructed dataset.

We've developed two probabilistic models for the COVID-19 pandemic. We've derived the statistical properties of these models, including correlation functions and probability distributions. These models, which build upon existing work and incorporate lockdown measures and the critical role of hospitals and health care facilities, enable policy makers to comprehend the impact of varying policies on outbreak trends. By analyzing correlations and probabilities, we can determine if lockdown measures are effective and if hospital capacity is sufficient to contain the virus. Following lockdown measures, we found the virus continues to spread, but at a slower rate, implying that measures such as "social distancing" are necessary for a long-term solution. Lockdown measures, however, provide temporary respite, implying that a mix of non-pharmaceutical interventions is required for control. After lockdown measures, we estimated that the virus takes around 80 weeks to reach its pre-lockdown mean and variance in certain health districts. Couple this with hospital capacity considerations, we can deduce that hospitalization can only slow the virus, and never halt it. We also discovered that a particular model, where susceptible individuals are less likely to contract the disease, results in reduced mean and variance, implying a potential solution, albeit temporary, for district health situations where hospital capacity is a concern. We further analyzed the SIS model, which reveals that removal of lockdown measures won't halt the virus. Only a temporary respite is won, but a respite that is limited in duration. Yet again the model confirms that a mix of

The ISGMR and ISGQR strengths are studied in deformable nuclei through the analysis of the isospin-fluctuation operator in the context of the Skyrme Hartree-Fock approach. A specific ISGMR strength is identified and observed to be correlated with the incompressibility modulus, but this relationship is weakened by the presence of an additional low-energy peak. A detailed examination reveals that this low-energy peak arises from the ground state harmonic vibration and is prominent in heavily deformed nuclei. Consequently, this signal may be challenging to distinguish from the primary ISGMR strength. To make comparisons with the 1200 MeV/fm$^6$ limit, the isoscalar monopole strength needs to be corrected for this effect, but this adjustment becomes uncertain for heavily deformed nuclei. To address this, a new approach is developed to isolate the ISGMR strength by removing the influence of the ground state harmonic vibration and isospin-constrained fluctuations. As an example, this method is applied to the isospin-fluctuation operator in the $^{36}$Si isotopes and it is found that even in the superfluid region, the ISGMR strength can be accurately determined and it preserves the linear relationship between the isospin-fluctuation operator and the incompressibility modulus for a narrow low-energy peak. Additionally, this treatment also allows for a comparison with the 1200 MeV/fm$^6$ limit even for heavily deformed

A study on stick-slip dynamics and the convergence of motion paths in systems governed by Coulomb friction is conducted. The existence of a universally accessible and attractive region, near an equilibrium state, is confirmed through analytical means. Theoretical findings reveal that the system can only converge asymptotically, involving multiple sequences of stick-slip cycles, regardless of the starting conditions. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical models through diverse examples of convergence.

A novel reinforcement learning method based on the actor-critic type has been developed to tackle portfolio hedging challenges for a variety of financial securities and derivatives using historical data only. Key aspects of this approach involve leveraging various derivative types such as forwards, futures, options, and taking into account factors such as trading costs, liquidity constraints and other frictions. This algorithm can effectively handle portfolios of any nature and features continuous action and state spaces with a risk-adjusted objective. Most notably, the model allows for optimal hedging without the need for additional training in diverse initial conditions, thereby saving significant processing resources. Furthermore, theoretical analysis of the Bellman equation confirms the existence of feasible solutions and highlights the connection to our previously established Deep Hedging framework.

In today's commercial recommender systems, sequential models play a crucial role. These models predict the items users are most likely to engage with by analyzing their previous platform interactions. Despite their importance, many of these models struggle to grasp the underlying motivations driving users' actions online, making intent modeling vital for user understanding and optimal long-term engagement. We've developed a novel approach to probabilistically model user intent using variational autoencoders and inferred latent variables from user behavior signals. Our approach then adjusts the recommendation policy accordingly, based on inferred user intent. We've validated the efficacy of our approach through offline and live testing on a massive industrial platform.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation stands out due to its unique unfolding into a Fuchsian equation through a general symmetric process. The Fuchsian equation resulting from the unfolding of this particular DCHE has five distinct singular points: three located near a vanishing parameter value, one corresponding to infinity, and another positioned at its reciprocal, as well as a fifth point at infinity. The monodromy matrix of the equation is calculated around the singular point at infinity, with the finding that the monodromy matrix is dependent on the parameters of the DCHE even after they are normalized. The matrix is further expressed in terms of the Inverno, M. A. M. Caron, and A. M. A. C. L. F. A. C. model in the context of Fuchsian equations. The research also identifies a specific subset of the DCHE that unfolds into the well-known Ablowitz-Lanford-Frank Ivlev-MacIntosh Fuchsian equation, notable for its appearance in the study of the Airy stationary water profile problem.

Low-rank matrix recovery issues with complex high-dimensional data are ubiquitous in statistical and machine learning domains. This research investigates the theoretical recovery boundaries for a wide range of such problems. We specifically address the challenge of estimating a matrix based on incomplete data with different levels of noise affecting separate components. We derive a universal recovery condition applicable to any non-parametric model that can be represented as a low-rank tensor. This condition relies on the concept of minimal separation between data elements, which we further demonstrate to be the dominant factor influencing recovery in each individual problem. We showcase our findings using real-world examples from brain imaging and document the corresponding numerical results.

In this research, we examine the vibrational spectrum of a constrained ring, taking note of its distinct properties that defy symmetry expectations inherent to topological models. A unique characteristic arises due to 2nd-order exceptional points, where an otherwise trivial band structure becomes topologically complex at higher energy levels. Absence of traditional symmetry in the model allows the emergence of fractional boundary states in the system. Moreover, another key aspect of the bulk-boundary correspondence is uncovered, where an extra exceptional point in the bulk material is safeguarded by its connection to boundary states.

We introduce the semi-inclusive Lepton Flavour Universality ratio $R_\Sigma$ to verify electron-to-muon universality in the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ process at $e^+e^-$ B-meson facilities. This combined observable enhances our capacity to detect potential violations of short distance origin Lepton Flavour Universality, all while retaining a straightforward theoretical explanation if a deviation from its predicted Standard Model value, $R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$, is observed.

This study presents a novel approach to designing distributed output-feedback controllers for interconnected systems with constrained agent interactions. Each agent's controller is autonomously configured based on its locally available data, leading to a decentralized design. Importantly, our approach can maintain stability even in the face of dynamic network reconfigurations, without requiring adjustments from other agents, thus ensuring seamless integration of new members and efficient controller upkeep. This robust design is enabled by leveraging Bass' algorithm to compute stabilizing controller gains through distributed solutions to Lyapunov equations.

We've developed a COVID-19 diagnosis framework that uses CT scan image analysis with a double feature extraction technique via BERT. The initial step utilizes a 3D-CNN to extract spatial information from the CT images and then employs BERT for temporal aggregation of these features. A classification model is trained using two randomly split validation sets, and a ranking model is trained on the remaining data in each split. A final diagnosis is made by combining the rankings from both models. A model was trained on 420 samples and demonstrated high accuracy, achieving a $AUROC$ of 0.9066 and $AUPRC$ of 0.866, performing significantly better than a baseline model which achieved an $AUPRC$ of 0.85 when applied to an independent test set of 340 unknown samples.

Network science is the multidisciplinary study of intricate systems, which can be represented as interconnected networks consisting of nodes and edges with various attributes. These seemingly straightforward structures conceal an extraordinary depth of complexity due to their capability to encapsulate a wide array of real-world phenomena, encompassing chemical reactions, biological pathways, social connections, and other intricate relationships. Mastering network science necessitates the mastery of a comprehensive and continually evolving set of techniques that span numerous academic disciplines, including graph and computer science, algebraic and statistical theories, physics, epidemiology, sociology, and other fields.

In this comprehensive resource, the collective expertise of the National Network Science Consortium will be shared, which comprises researchers from diverse academic and industrial backgrounds. This knowledge is compiled into six primary chapters, which cover a wide range of network science techniques. These foundational concepts are then applied in several illustrative case studies, which demonstrate the strategic implementation of these methods to solve complex problems. Additionally, the consortium will make available a suite of open-source software tools to support each chapter, enabling curious minds to delve into the respective techniques through hands-on experiences.

This document serves as a comprehensive guide that bridges the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application, while also fostering further innovation by providing open-source software and promoting hands-on learning.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is being limited by an exclusive focus on fast-changing ecology and evolution, typically occurring over short periods, in simple systems. This has the consequence of excluding these processes from longer-term models of global change and making them inaccessible to observers with timescales of centuries. To address this issue, we have developed a hierarchical theory of eco-evolutionary dynamics for timescales ranging from seconds to millions of years. This framework recognizes that there are distinct timescales for different aspects of eco-evolutionary dynamics and allows for a step-by-step extension to longer-term processes. We have applied this theory to the study of long-term global change (over millions of years) and eco-evolutionary dynamics observed during a rapid climate event in 1815. Our analysis has demonstrated that timescales of millions of years could lead to the self-organization of eco-evolutionary dynamics and result in the emergence of patterns such as competition for limited resources and the evolution of species' interactions as a consequence of changes in species' traits.

A recently established benchmark called SUPERB drives research into learning speech representations by comparing various speech models with minimal adjustments to improve downstream performance. By showing that self-supervised speech models can excel in multiple downstream tasks with little adaptation, SUPERB highlights a significant paradigm in the speech field that needs to be studied more. Specifically, assessing the ability of speech models to resist malicious attacks under the control of knowledgeable and inexperienced adversaries has become a high priority in the speech community. In this research, we make a first effort to test the potential vulnerability of speech models to both types of adversaries through experiments that generate effective countermeasures. The experiments show that speech models developed in the SUPERB paradigm are particularly susceptible to attacks launched by adversaries lacking extensive knowledge, and the crafted attacks by expert adversaries exhibit portability across various scenarios. Moreover, our XAB testing process confirms the undetectability of generated attacks by adversaries.

Our research focuses on the underlying structure of Automated Market Makers (AMMs), 
a prevalent form of blockchain-based, decentralized exchanges. 
We reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. 
AMMs are adopted predominantly when their supported token portfolios have significant components of pairs that are frequently traded together, giving us a novel explanation for the volatility-driven adoption rate. 
Using actual data from AMMs and tokens, our findings are supported, along with two additional facts: the majority of tokens from existing AMMs exhibit negative value changes, and low-cap tokens are more likely to be part of less commonly traded pairs.

We develop and analyze a mathematical model describing AMMs' order processing mechanisms in terms of their underlying structure. This framework allows us to investigate the underlying properties of AMMs, a task that is not facilitated by the existing literature. Our research focuses on the order processing mechanism of AMMs, a blockchain-based, decentralized exchange type, to reveal that the order processing mechanism results in token value diminishment for market liquidity suppliers under circumstances of heightened token price volatility. This phenomenon is attributed to an increase in token exchange rate volatility in AMMs, a phenomenon that is not observed in a matched firm pair. Our findings are derived from actual data and used to explore the underlying structure of AMMs, a task that is not facilitated by the existing literature.

A new analytical framework, referred to as Sensitivity Analysis, assesses how conclusions derived from complete data sets hold up in the presence of missing information. In order to evaluate the impact of data limitations on findings from traditional frequency and probability statistics, researchers must establish upper bounds on their potential distortion. In contrast, we introduce a novel approach, which employs a model-based metric to gauge the influence of data completeness on research conclusions by directly estimating distortion levels. A discrete Bayesian network framework is utilized to capture the relationships between variables, particularly one that accommodates multiple types of missing data (item response theory). The analysis of over 100,000 questionnaires from Taiwan serves as a real-world example of our proposed methodology, with calculations performed using the Bayesian Monte Carlo algorithm. The results demonstrate the interplay between different types of missing data and indicate that different parameters are largely insulated from each other. The implications of our findings are explored further.

This review summarizes the breakdown of the eigenvalue problem for a combined system of the Wilson loop and the Gubin-Khomskii model, alongside a companion paper that details the solution for two specific representations of $U_q(\sl2)$. Our approach relies on the reduction of the given problem using the Cartan generator's action, which results in a hierarchy of diabatic quantum systems. This quantum structure is then analyzed by exploring its quantum geometry defined by interrelated quantum spaces, where the Euler-Angel polynomial generates the corresponding quantum groups $U_q(\sl2)$. Moreover, for the rep-$U_q(\sl2)$ representation, the hierarchy demonstrates the emergence of two distinct limits, which can be thought of as equivalent to a quantum $\mathbb Z_N$ gauge theory and a quantum SDW/HS model, respectively.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

The ALICE experiment has recorded the $p_\mathrm{T}$ distribution of D meson production, including both prompt and non-prompt (formed in beauty-hadron decays), in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, and analyzed it with an enhanced data set, yielding the same results as previous studies at a different energy point. The findings show that non-prompt meson production is consistent with theoretical models and earlier data in the measured $p_\mathrm{T}$ range. An enhanced data set has also allowed the creation of two distinct $p_\mathrm{T}$ distributions for D meson production: one for mesons created directly in particle collisions and another for those created in the presence of a quark or antiquark. The analysis has also led to an estimation of the nuclear modification factor for D meson production in the most central collisions and revealed an average suppression factor of about 20-30% compared to theoretical models.

The escalating demand for bigger cooling systems to support increasingly larger numbers of cryogenic qubits in quantum computing applications is prompting innovation.
Through the National Quantum Initiative and Department of Energy's support, our work at the Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems Center at Fermilab aims to create a 2-meter diameter by approximately 1.5-meter tall experimental space capable of achieving extremely low millikelvin temperatures within a few hundred liters of volume.
This effort involves designing and developing a cutting-edge, ultra-low-vacuum-based cryogenic platform featuring two distinct cryogenic stages, each utilizing a unique cooling technique.
One stage utilizes a conventional system with liquid helium-3 cooling and thermal insulation, while the second stage employs a massive heatswitch to transition to an ultra-cold stage utilizing a multi-layer superconducting thermal-superconductor-normal conductor thermal-superconductor (TLS) system that leverages the properties of superconducting materials to achieve exceptional thermal stability.
Details of our experimental layout, platform design, and initial test results will be discussed, including the significance of an exceptionally stable thermal environment and the potential impact on quantum bit coherence times.

Previous research indicates a high prevalence of misused crypto APIs in Java and C, but similar studies for other languages have been absent, with one notable exception - a study conducted on professional developers in Python revealed a lower incidence of insecure code for crypto-related tasks. Researchers have employed the depyzer tool to audit 100 popular Python projects and found that nearly 90% exhibit at least one instance of crypto API misuse. These findings demonstrate that the majority of such projects pose data security risks due to potential vulnerabilities in their code. We have also developed a classification system for assessing the severity of security flaws in crypto code. Our study provides new insights into the working practices of Python developers regarding crypto code security and suggests that most projects could benefit from improved training and support to strengthen their security standards.

This paper presents an effective approach for locating fixed three-dimensional objects within large-scale metropolitan landscapes using an aggregation strategy for substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data, yielding significantly enhanced precision and robustness. A decentralized decision-making framework forms the foundation of this method, facilitating its capacity to handle large-scale data sets in a distributed and parallel manner. Evaluating this method with extensive image collections, encompassing nearly 400,000 images across 40 square kilometers of New York City and San Francisco, demonstrates its capacity to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional coordinates of objects, such as streetlights. Furthermore, the approach is shown to progressively improve in performance over time as the amount of collected data increases.

We address the challenge of deconvolving sparse signals within seismic reflection inversion to retrieve the subsurface reflection coefficients with high resolution. Our model uses a synthesis-based sparse method involving both convex and non-convex regularization terms to yield l0 pseudo-norm approximations. This leads to an iterative algorithm using proximal averaging that can be reformatted as a trainable neural network, optimizing a energy function inspired by our regularized optimization problem. By employing a weighted l1-regularization, we can control the level of sparsity and also generate a trainable thresholding function at the training stage. Additionally, we can increase the potential of deep learning by iteratively updating our algorithm's output. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm, especially in terms of wave equation-based inversion where it surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning techniques and traditional optimization algorithms.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. In the context of BMOA_p, where 0 < p < 1, several findings stand out. Firstly, different semigroups exhibit varied properties - some are invariant, some are not, and certain are closed while others are not. Notably, in the BMOA space (p = 1), the semigroup of composition operators under the norm is not a Banach algebra. However, it is a topological left semigroup. Key conclusions regarding the topological right semigroup of composition operators under the norm are also established. Furthermore, this article explores the characteristics of Banach semigroups of composition operators with respect to BMOA_p's dual space. In the case of p < 1, it is revealed that such a semigroup is an RLBMOA_p subspace. In the case of p = 1, it is discovered that this condition holds for the right strongly continuous semigroups. Finally, this article proves the equivalence of two topologies on the space of BMOA_p composition operators.

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires identifying key components of conformal field theory, notably the coefficients of operator product expansion, which describe operator fusion. Research suggests these coefficients can be computed using a wavefunction formed from two-dimensional wavefunctions at a specific infinite-natured point. However, conventional methods for evaluating this wavefunction are hindered by computational challenges associated with the rank of the matrix, even with moderate chain lengths. However, we've found that using a wavefunction expressed as a linear combination of operator matrix product states, we can overcome these computational limitations. Our work has led to new results for XQZ models, confirming predictions based on the analytic properties of the conformal dimension. Similarly, we've obtained results for the higher rank $su(2)_1 \oplus su(2)_2$ Wess-Zumino-Witten models with an infinite-natured point.

Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing. Although POS tagging has been successfully achieved for many modern languages, the case for historical corpora is vastly different. Limited resources and complex variation in historical word forms present significant obstacles. In response to these challenges, we have developed a robust and generalized framework for automatically tagging historical texts, which can be adapted to new corpora with relative ease. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach, achieving high accuracy rates comparable to those for contemporary languages, through applications in two existing corpora. Furthermore, the output of our POS tagging pipeline is made available to the research community, accompanying a paper that is soon to be published. The respective DOIs are 10.3366/HCUAH.2023.0002 and 10.3366/HCUAH.2023.0003.

This research focuses on developing a method to calculate a utility function from a non-differentiable but locally-representable candidate of a demand function. Using this method, we derive two new criteria that a non-differentiable candidate must meet to be considered a valid demand function. One criterion checks for a specific relation between a small change in a commodity bundle and a small change in a consumer's utility, while the other criterion examines the relation between a consumer's utility and their satiation level. Additionally, under certain conditions, we show that a locally-concave demand function can be used to construct a valid utility function by applying a specific method. Our results also provide insight into the characteristics of an ideal candidate for a demand function. One such ideal candidate is a specifically designed piecewise-affine demand function, which we demonstrate can be used to construct a valid utility function for any concave income curve.

As smart cities expand, they generate a greater need for automated conversion of human-specified demands into precise, machine-readable specifications. Nevertheless, a considerable number of requirements still originate from individuals who aren't utilizing any form of interactive visual assistance. We have developed CitySpec, an intelligent assistant for smart city infrastructure administrators, which facilitates the conversion of natural language-based demands into API requests for accessible, visual interface support. By leveraging the potential of pre-trained models, specifically Text-to-Image Models (T2IGs), like Egohms, which capitalize on advancements in image-text pairing pre-training, we have successfully enhanced our system to effectively generate human-like outcomes. Our experimental findings showcase that Egohms outperform the current model Egocyc in producing high-quality specifications that are also evaluated positively by users.

Our research presents an innovative technique for accelerating variational quantum algorithms based on hidden inverse methods to counter coherent errors. By executing an error-correcting inverse gate before the final measurement, we bypass the necessity for a precise inverse gate implementation, thereby reducing the impact of coherent errors in the following ways: (1) by eliminating any bias caused by the two-point correlation function, (2) by heavily suppressing the standard zero-point fluctuation term, and most importantly, (3) by transforming the Hamiltonian into a commutator form post-processing, thereby greatly reducing the impact of coherent errors at the readout stage. Through our methods, error reduction can be achieved with just one additional gate before measurement, a move highly beneficial for Lattice Gauge Theory simulations in the realm of quantum computing.

In a general category $\mathbb E$, taking the direct image of a partial order under a surjective epimorphism may not yield a partial order. In the category of sets, the best partial order approximation of the image in such a case is obtained by forming the cofibered image of the original preorder above the epimorphism. In categories satisfying regularity conditions, the existence of such a cofibered image of a partial order corresponds to the existence of the least upper bound among all partial orders within the category. This work explores conditions ensuring the existence of these cofibered images, which can be used in two distinct areas of study: the context of topoi with suprema of subobject chains or the context of $n$-permutable categories.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a range of 600 to 800 kilometers.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn transferable visual representations. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by semantic inconsistencies between datasets. To optimize visual-textual alignment for CLIP models on various tasks, we introduce a technique that refines image-text cross-modality learning via VT-CLIP. This process involves utilizing attention-driven mechanisms to direct text features toward informative visual regions, effectively enhancing visual-textual correlation for improved category-based matching. Subsequently, we demonstrate VT-CLIP's efficacy in few-shot classification scenarios, observing an improvement of at least +9% and up to +21% in top-1 accuracy compared to baseline methods. Our source code can be found at https://github.com/ko6an/VT-CLIP.

To enhance the accuracy of computational models plagued by noisy data and parameters, this study addresses the issue of reducing error in a linear system affected by uncertainty. By building upon Etter and Ying's '20 elliptic operator shifting framework, we extend this concept to a broader range of matrices, specifically nonsymmetric elliptic matrices, within the context of the least-squares problem. This revised framework is based on a new theoretical conclusion and utilizes the shifted matrix, whose least-singular value is bounded by a given error margin, to determine a suitable approximate solution. A numerical example demonstrating the improved precision of this approach is also presented.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of integral suspensions of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where the spectra of the form $H\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ are considered, and the equivariance group in question is the quaternionic group $Q_8$. The 1986 work by Chase and Quick, as well as a later paper by Harper in 1990, computed the homotopy groups of $Q_8$-spheres up to a certain degree, extending Brown's findings. We have extended these results, computed the equivariant homotopy groups of $Q_8$-spheres for all degrees and established the existence of equivariant Bott sets. The work presented here offers a direct computational method that can be used to determine the slices of the equivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, where we have observed that the slices are in fact nonequivariant Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra, and this has been done for any equivariance group for which the order has a certain form, and the group itself is a 2-group.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the depth of this ideal and its relation to this parameter. These criteria also offer a test for idealistic algebras in terms of this parameter's depth, which is an extension of a prior theorem by Pherrett. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our $F$-rationality criteria result in a more streamlined form for the $F$-pure threshold in certain situations. Lastly, this criteria also provides a basis for identifying the types of rings that satisfy the equation $(S_2,\text{R})\Rightarrow\text{F-rational}$.

The application of machine learning in image diagnostics within pathology and radiology is growing rapidly.  Despite its promise, accessing and labeling sufficient medical images to train sophisticated machine learning algorithms proves difficult and costly.  The medical imaging community often relies on the ANSI/ISO/IEC-12873 standard, known as DICOM, to share images, along with associated medical data, across systems of differing compatibility.  This paper will explore various methods of processing, simplifying, and visualizing images labeled in accordance with the standard, in order to facilitate the use of machine learning algorithms.  The paper will provide specific examples of utilizing the Pydicom library to access, decode, and retrieve image data, as well as demonstrate strategies for standardizing image displays across diverse medical devices.  Additionally, the paper will highlight efficient data representation methods that enable the rapid training of deep learning algorithms.  Finally, the paper will showcase approaches for labeling and processing data that make it suitable for the application of quantitative machine learning techniques to medical images.

We present a derivation of Noether's current from the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term and demonstrate that the corresponding charge is connected to Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, when evaluated on the horizon. The entropy can also be calculated using a Virasoro algebra and Cardy formula approach, in which we identify relevant diffeomorphisms based on a simple physical principle that maintains the horizon structure's invariance. Our method complements earlier research and utilizes the York-Gibbons-Hawking surface term to reach a similar conclusion, thereby providing technical and physical advancements.

In recent times, deep learning has significantly impacted the field of sequence representation. However, the field of genomics is particularly challenging due to sequences of vastly differing lengths. A primary goal in the area of long and variable DNA sequence learning involves discovering a suitable fixed dimension representation for DNA sequences of varying lengths. This paper presents an unsupervised DNA sequence learning approach that uses a fixed number of dimensions with a primary goal of obtaining a more effective representation. The DNA sequence is initially encoded using a convolutional network and then passed through an unsupervised learning technique called autoencoders. A large DNA sequence is fed into the encoding part of the convolutional network to obtain a summary encoding. This encoding is then represented as a matrix known as T-POT. Subsequent applications of the convolutional network encode the T-POT matrix, producing a new encoding known as the NPT. The NPT matrix is then given to a supervised learning approach where the classification of DNA sequences into different types takes place, utilizing a technique known as the convolutional neural networks. The findings indicate that the proposed method has a high degree of accuracy in the classification of sequences of varying lengths.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the impact of surface termination.  Our research achieved control over the surface termination of V$_2$O$_3$ films during growth using low-energy evaporation, resulting in high-quality films grown on TaO$_2$/Ta(001).  Evolution of the film phase with thickness was examined using a combination of techniques including X-ray diffraction, resonant soft X-ray scattering, and low-energy electron diffraction.  Films grown under a variety of conditions exhibited a phase-pure α-phase (a = 4.37 Å) with a monoclinic distortion (c = 2.91 Å) are not dependent on the substrate.  However, it is discovered that the distance between layers (c) is contingent on the substrate (4.37 Å > c/t > 2.91 Å).
