Utilizing a range of resonant soft X-ray scattering conditions, it is demonstrated that the films exhibit a metallic electronic state not contingent on thickness or surface oxidation state.  Our research reveals the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ is controlled by surface oxidation and can be achieved through exposure to oxygen.  Our research indicates the metal-insulator transition is a consequence of charge transfer at the surface, altering the oxidation state of the next layer and introducing

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Furthermore, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson systems collectivization. Consequently, applying symplectic Runge-Kutta integrators to the newly formed Hamiltonian systems results in collecting the original Lie-Poisch equations' solutions into a single curve. We provide both an algebraic and a geometric justification for this result.

The analysis of microlensing events offers the best method for learning about the galactic distribution of exoplanets, especially their masses. Since 2017, the galactic-scale Spitzer survey has yielded ten events whose posterior distributions are now usable for statistical analysis. Conducting a statistical comparison between the observed outcomes and theoretical microlensing models, this study found that these outcomes match the expected results 87% of the time, using a likelihood ratio test to evaluate the data's fit to different models. Furthermore, this study's findings indicate that the galactic distribution of exoplanets has a mass ratio greater than 0.1 for super-Earth objects and a mass ratio greater than 0.03 for Neptune-like objects, with these constraints being more precise than prior estimates. Finally, the predicted abundance of exoplanets with a mass ratio greater than 0.1 will be verified using the predicted abundance of giant exoplanets derived from the galactic model fitting, with this prediction made independently of the mass ratio prior.

To address a category of optimal control issues for hyperbolic conservation law systems and their regularization versions through viscosity, a comprehensive approach is proposed and implemented. This approach is illustrated through the analysis of a canonical example, heat equation-based optimal control problems, to establish a deeper understanding of these types of problems.

Accurately predicting non-performing loans for individual clients is a key factor for banks to mitigate credit risk and make informed lending decisions.
This process is typically based on comprehensive borrower profiles, including information on loan proposals and personal histories.
Previous research has found that certain factors like employee client loan applications are particularly challenging to predict.
We aim to refine NPL predictions by focusing on the loan applicant's attributes and utilizing the attention mechanism to weigh the significance of each feature.
Experimental results using a Croatian bank's data show that (i) applicant-centric NPL predictions yield better accuracy, (ii) the most important applicant characteristics are age, years with the bank, and employment status, and (iii) the attention mechanism provides valuable insights into feature contributions.
We observe a 2.5% improvement in NPL prediction accuracy using this methodology over traditional models.

The connections between the chromatic symmetric functions of specific Dyck paths, originally discovered by Stanley and later expanded on by Shareshian-Wachs in their $q$-analogue, are crucial in their associations with Hessenberg varieties, diagonal harmonics, and LLT polynomials. Notably, for the so-called deformed Dyck paths related to type $A$ shifted non-attacking rooks, a direct link to shifted symmetizable tableaux is established, thereby answering a question posed by Garsia-Rotolo-Thomassen. Furthermore, the results achieved are achieved within an established $e$-plane involution framework, allowing for its application in an ongoing effort to develop a bijective proof for the $q$-analogue of Stanley's result. The approach employed involves an innovative application of the "insertion-evacuation" method developed by Guo-Neiman.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are constructed by selecting key Gabor filters and expressing them as sparse linear combinations of these selected filters. Through noise scheduling and regularization, we enable the learning of these Landmark Features in a sparse and non-linear manner. Our experimental results show that OCNs outperform traditional DCNNs in terms of both accuracy and classification speed.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character. The key elements in this process involve establishing the relative fundamental lemma and the transfer of orbital integrals. Coupled with the spectral isolation technique pioneered by Beuzart-Plessis--Liu--Zhang--Zhu, we derive comparisons of the elliptic aspects of the involved relative trace formulas, ultimately yielding novel outcomes that extend Waldspurger's theorem to the scenario where n is equal to 1.

We develop a systematic method to manage the uncertainty associated with heavy quark flavors, which arises when using different masses to describe the same flavor. Using perturbation theory up to four loops, we create a framework for evading this limitation and establish a precise range of acceptable masses for the bottom and top quarks, taking into account standard model parameters and the characteristics of next-to-next-to-next-to leading order QCD predictions. Specifically, for the bottom quark, we confirm a 40 MeV range of acceptable masses, whereas for the top quark, which is essentially unaffected by perturbative corrections, any mass within a particular renormalization scheme is considered acceptable. Additionally, we lay out a strategy to further mitigate the uncertainty and bring the pole mass calculation even closer to precision. We further expand upon this work by examining the mass range for the bottom quark in non-commensurate renormalization schemes and evaluating the decay rate of the bottom quark into a W boson, taking into account various schemes and the accuracy of low-energy observables in reproducing the pole mass.

Consider a graph $G$ and a subset $R$ of its vertices $V(G)$.  A specific edge coloring known as $R$-sequential $t$-coloring occurs when each vertex in $R$ is given a number from 1 to $t$, with adjacent vertices receiving consecutive numbers and adjacent edges getting consecutive numbers starting from a specific vertex in $R$. This concept leads to a more complex idea called $R$-sequential $t$-factor which is a specific edge multiplication factor involving the vertices in $R$. This paper explores different conditions under which $R$-sequential $R$-colorings and $R$-sequential $t$-colorings exist and also investigates the requirements for an $R$-sequential $t$-factor to occur. Through this exploration, we establish a number of useful results which contribute to our understanding of these concepts while also providing constructive proof methods that can be used to create these sequences.

We establish a precise relationship between L^p to L^q contraction inequalities in weighted Bergman spaces over the unit disk, incorporating typical weight factors and α > 1. This outcome addresses an unresolved issue in reference \cite{JANSON}, with the added consideration of cases where q is greater than or equal to 2, while providing related estimates for 0 < q < 2.

Currently, the most trusted diagnostic tool for COVID-19 is RT-PCR, which
takes several days and sometimes produces inaccurate results. Computed Tomography
scans can also identify respiratory abnormalities by displaying lung density in
three dimensions. Although high-quality CT scans can detect COVID-19 lesions, the
scarcity of personal protective equipment and the risk of infection has created a
demand for low-dose and ultra-low-dose scans that balance image analysis with
reduced exposure. This study evaluates a neural network approach to analyze
low-dose and ultra-low-dose CT scans without compromising diagnostic accuracy.
By using a relatively small dataset of 150 standard-dose CT scans, the model
reaches an impressive sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 95%, also demonstrating
better outcomes than several top-tier COVID-19 detection models using large datasets
of unprocessed CT scans. Computed Tomography scans can also identify pulmonary
pathology in smokers. This study was conducted in collaboration with a local
hospital.

As numerous satellite constellations in the low-Earth orbit region are scheduled to launch, effectively arranging the space occupied by each satellite in their operational trajectories is essential to prevent collisions and reduce critical encounters. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen-orbit initial conditions in osculating element space were derived and further analyzed in the context of several frozen orbits. Furthermore, frozen-orbit initial conditions were derived for all valid frozen orbits, resulting in a set of proper eccentricity values. Moreover, it is found that satellites in the same space occupancy group have identical or closely related eccentricities, thereby demonstrating the potential to significantly reduce the number of required eccentricities by co-orbiting multiple satellites. Finally, a method to arrange constellation elevations based on space occupancy is presented, thereby addressing the challenge of arranging the space occupied by each satellite in an optimal manner.

To generate top-quality quadrilateral meshes on complex computer-aided design (CAD) models efficiently, we propose an integrated solution. A versatile mesh with numerous irregular points is initially created using Delaunay triangulation. Subsequently, a more refined quadrilateral mesh is derived by incrementally introducing new points, which are carefully selected to maintain high-order mesh quality. To achieve this, we tailor and apply existing mesh quality metrics originally designed for tetrahedral meshes to the framework of unstructured quadrilateral meshes. As a result, we offer a robust and efficient method for producing high-order quadrilateral meshes on intricate CAD surfaces across various numerical domains.

Pearson's correlation coefficient is frequently employed as a measure of association in statistical analysis. The strength of evidence for linear correlation between two variables is typically evaluated using a t-statistic, followed by a calculation of a p-value based on a assumed confidence interval. However, as we demonstrate in this study, these techniques can be overly conservative, particularly when the data sets in question are small. An alternative testing method is proposed here, grounded in a approach by Anders Eschenauer referred to as the'regression for growth periods' method, which is subsequently adapted for use in conventional software programs for statistical analysis. The proposed test exhibits superior power in comparison to the traditional approach, with results indicating a lower rate of Type II errors. Additionally, this method is seen to offer benefits in a range of other domains.

We detail the reasoning behind implementing a quantum S-matrix approach for tackling classical gravitational scattering between two bodies. Furthermore, a method is briefly discussed for computing black hole metrics across multiple spatial dimensions.

We investigate the two- or three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations defined within a bounded region. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls in the vicinity of an unstable equilibrium in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces that approximate L^3(Omega) spaces where Omega is a three-dimensional domain. The outcome of our work is the first to provide practical solutions for controlling the Navier-Stokes equations in 3D space using local controls in the sense of PDEs. In order to achieve this, we employed the concept of weak solution in the context of the Navier-Stokes equations and overcame the issue of finite dimensional feedback control that falls short in addressing the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations in the sense of energy space. The argument we presented avoids the use of logarithmic terms in the context of $L^3(\Omega)$ spaces where Omega is a one-dimensional domain. Language learning dictionaries can facilitate vocabulary acquisition by supplying 
word definitions, although conventional dictionaries may struggle with 
capturing word meanings that vary across specific contexts. A potential solution 
is introduced in this study: the LitMind Dictionary, an online dictionary platform 
accessible through a web interface. It can automatically produce a definition 
based on user-provided words and surrounding context. Furthermore, the LitMind 
Dictionary supports multilingual queries, enabling the generation of definitions 
for Chinese and English, as well as cross-language inquiries between these two 
languages. A simplified user interface enables quick lookup of words and phrases 
using a mouse or by copying and pasting them into the web interface.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for intricate models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have exposed limitations in local surrogate-based post-hoc explanations regarding their inherent reliability, especially in critical applications such as human-centric recommendation tasks. Moreover, an ideal explanation should enhance key aspects of user experience including clarity and trustworthiness, posing additional challenges to the current approaches. However, a classical post-hoc model utilizing surrogates demonstrates dependence on the model itself, distilling only the surrogate, rather than the actual decision-making mechanism. In our proposed Argo framework, we address these limitations by adopting a generative adversarial network to create a more reliable user-centric post-hoc explanation. Our proposed explanations focus on accurately representing the decision-making reasoning behind recommended items and categorizing unselected ones. Comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets have shown Argo's effectiveness in significantly improving user understanding and trust in the recommendations provided.

Quantum devices based on superconducting properties may be effectively produced
using semiconductor-superconductor hybrids, consisting of materials in close
contact and a well-formed connection. The surface energy levels of materials like
InAs, characterized by a bandgap significantly smaller than the Fermi
level, are particularly influential. As a result, achieving strong electronic
conduction along the interface between InAs and a superconductor like NbI3
invokes the need for microscopic examinations of the interface. The surface
morphology plays a crucial part in determining conductivity, as evident from
scanning tunneling microscopy studies of the NbI3 surface, revealing numerous
holes, but also showing that these defects do not significantly affect electronic
conduction. The device consists of an stacked heterostructure of InAs, InAsSb,
NbI3, and NbN layers, each about 2 nm in thickness. The resulting electronic
current density displays the characteristics of a well-formed density of states
at the interface, as indicated by a non-linear coefficient of 0.52 ± 0.2 meV.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the learnability of dense concept learning models. Therefore, a more conservative approach has been developed, focusing on deriving learnability results for a basic dense concept class under minimal assumptions. A robust model was created that can handle adversarially corrupted data without making any assumptions about its distribution. Additionally, this model was enhanced by deriving the first dense concept learning results for a robust model that handles an adversary and incorporates local membership queries.

Our previous research significantly accelerated the solution of the continuous-time linear system by implementing a log-time pre-conditioner, but this came with the limitation of being applicable only to lower/upper triangular colexhoff matrices. This paper builds upon that research, presenting an algorithm that efficiently handles left/right triangular colexhoff matrices in log time. The proposed method for solving continuous-time linear systems relies on a combination of the log-time pre-conditioner for triangular matrices and the existing fast solution methods for non-triangular matrices. Moreover, under the assumption of random sampling, the new approach permits a wide range of linear combinations of the input vectors while maintaining a fast solution time, particularly for non-triangular matrices. Furthermore, the paper shows that triangular colexhoff matrices are capable of supporting a range of linear transformations without incurring a significant computational cost, resulting in efficient performance for a class of systems involving multiple right-hand sides.

Young stars emitting intense X-ray and UV radiation can drastically alter planetary atmospheres, influencing both mass loss and chemistry. Observing AU Mic, an active 22-million-year-old star hosting two planets inside its debris disk, presents an extraordinary chance to examine these impacts in detail. Utilizing the Advanced Stellar interferometer System at the Thirty Meter Telescope, we aim to construct 3D models of the star's corona, while analyzing AU Mic's temporal variability in X-ray and the far-UV spectral range (10 nm - 360 nm) may reveal crucial insights into its photochemistry, circumplanetary disk evolution, and potential habitability.

We develop an innovative approach to describe the friction caused by radiation experienced by particles moving through a medium with mechanical resistance. We introduce an effect where the medium is warped by the motion of charged particles in a way that the Larmor formula accurately describes the energy lost due to radiation. We compare this description to a different model that has some similarities to the Landau-Lifshitz model and find that the other model exhibits non-physical behavior. Our new method suggests that the energy lost due to radiation will be limited by the energy lost due to mechanical resistance in the medium when the friction is very strong. We also demonstrate that significant amounts of soft radiation can be generated by particles interacting strongly with each other, for example, when quarks interact in a quark-gluon plasma, leading to mechanical friction.

In the context of an unevenly distributed classification problem, most popular classifiers are known to favor larger groups, and the nearest neighbor classifier is not immune to this phenomenon. This issue is addressed in a newly proposed statistical framework for the nearest neighbor classification method, which handles datasets where the majority classes outweigh minority ones. Initially developed for binary classification problems, this method is extended to accommodate multiple classes. Unlike existing over-sampling techniques that involve generating fake data points, this method achieves replicable results by sidestepping pseudo observation generation. Moreover, this method has demonstrated Bayesian risk consistency when subjected to relevant conditions and shows significant improvement in its performance compared to other existing methods, all backed up by a comprehensive analysis of several reference datasets.

We employ photometry data from multiple sources to identify ultra-bright Quasi-Stellar Objects (QSOs) located at distant regions of space. Following a detailed description of our data processing methods, we succeed in isolating over 1,600 QSO candidates across nearly 1,300 square degrees. From the spectra of more than 1,000 QSO candidates, we determine their redshift values, enabling us to calculate the QSO luminosity function and its intrinsic slope based on a particular luminosity reference. Furthermore, we calculate the number density of QSOs at different redshift values and compare our findings to previous studies, revealing some discrepancies at certain redshift points with the existing research, yet with wide measurement errors when compared to other studies. Additionally, based on the QSO number density evolution suggested by our QSO luminosity function data, we infer that the peak QSO activity occurred around z equal to 2.9, consistent with the results from other research.

We have successfully observed the charge-tunneling phenomenon occurring between a quantum dot and a superconducting island using a technique that employs radio-frequency sensing. Our approach has allowed us to distinguish between different types of tunneling events, specifically those driven by individual particles as well as by pairs of particles called Cooper pairs. Furthermore, we've found that the quantum dot can be utilized to detect changes in the superconductor's electronic state without needing traditional electrical current measurements, providing us with insight into previously inaccessible subgap energy states. Our findings offer valuable insights for future research focused on detecting parity-dependent interactions between these quantum dots and superconducting islands, potentially revealing the existence of elusive Majorana modes.

Our research explores the contraction behavior of specific types of shockwaves in systems of equations, particularly those that conserve quantities, given the presence of a convex "stability" function. To expand upon existing work, we introduce a new metric that can accommodate spatial variations and use it to establish conditions under which shockwaves in a broader class of systems, such as fluid flow equations, will behave predictably. Furthermore, we identify specific criteria that certain types of shockwaves must meet in order to be expected to behave predictably. Our investigation into these conditions includes the study of two-fluid dynamics models with and without magnetic forces, as well as fluid flow equations, for which we analyze the interaction between different types of shockwaves under various scenarios.

We explore novel view generation using diffusion models, which contend that the nested structure of an image hierarchy can facilitate generation of detailed information at longer ranges. To investigate this, we investigate two datasets with a focus on generating extended scenes one layer at a time in a hierarchical manner. Our results show that hierarchical conditioning of images on conditional diffusion models surpasses previous generative techniques that utilize GANs, including methods that employ style-based generators and semantic segment conditioning. Additionally, our findings indicate that previous long-range generators could not produce statistically credible results and suffered from severe image reconstruction errors. In contrast, our conditional diffusion models enable a grounded and incremental generation of scenes over multiple levels with Hierarchical datasets. Our work suggests that the nested structure of an image hierarchy can facilitate generation of detailed information at longer ranges. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/arnaldocastillo/conditionaldiffusion.

Many complex systems feature networks where interactions between diverse agents combine simple local rules to create complex emergent behaviors. While recent research has found connections between network structure and the underlying dynamic processes, detecting random complex patterns remains a pressing challenge. We develop a data-driven approach to uncover the underlying stochastic nonlinear dynamics in complex networks by using statistical inference to estimate dynamics in finite state spaces. This method, based on a information-theoretic criterion, identifies the most likely model among various options, even in the face of limited data. In realistic tests across different settings, this approach successfully recovers the underlying dynamics, although it can be challenging when multiple plausible models are available or when only fragmented information about the dynamics is available. Despite the challenges, this method significantly outperforms existing methods that infer dynamics in network problems. We apply this method to a study of the spread of COVID-19 through contact tracing and a investigation into the electoral sharing patterns of American Electors in 2020, demonstrating its ability to uncover the underlying stochastic nonlinear dynamics in complex networks.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber undergoing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability. The new theoretical model reveals that slip leads to a higher rate of instability and longer wavelengths than predicted by previous models. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. The accuracy of the theoretical model is supported by numerical simulations and experimental results from a study conducted by Haefner, et al., published in 2015 in Nature Communications.

We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, focusing on $\alpha$-dissipative solutions with $\alpha$ a constant in the interval $[0,1]$. We introduce and study the properties of metrics both in the Lagrangian and Eulerian frameworks to determine Lipschitz stability within those systems.

Evaluating scoliosis with ultrasound imaging is particularly difficult for individuals without prior experience. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with controlled pressure to accurately follow spinal curvature. This method was tested against manual scanning by examining the spinous process angles in 23 scoliosis patients using ultrasound. The results showed significant correlation between robotic and manual scans, with mean correlation coefficients of 0.96 for both approaches. Both approaches showed similar reliability when measuring scoliosis using ultrasound. This approach shows potential to reduce variability when measuring scoliosis using ultrasound.

This paper introduces an innovative duration modeling approach for statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) using a method that combines the strengths of mean and median estimators in modeling speech DUR. The traditional GMM approach often relies on mean-based duration predictions, but we observe that this method can fall short, particularly in contexts where duration variability is limited and biased towards means rather than medians. To address this limitation, we have developed an unbiased GMM approach called the Unbiased Gaussian Model (UGM). The UGM is capable of accurately modeling the median duration, thereby maintaining a low type-I error rate and achieving improved synthesis naturalness in experiments. The experimental findings reveal that this new UGM yields a type-I error rate of less than 0.05, while also yielding a significant improvement in synthesis naturalness, roughly estimated at a 9% increase in MOS scores compared to the traditional GMM approach.

Identifying online hate speech is increasingly critical due to its capacity to inflict emotional and psychological harm on minority groups. A recent study from TU Berlin's research team analyzed the performance of different Natural Language Processing models on subtasks one and two of the 2021 Indo-European language shared task, which focused on detecting hate speech and derogatory content. Our team assessed the effectiveness of models that rely on word and character-based recurrent neural networks and those employing BERT, a more sophisticated pre-trained model. Analysis revealed that models leveraging the BERT model exhibited better accuracy in identifying hate speech and derogatory content. A key finding also showed that BERT models outperformed those based on recurrent neural networks alone in predicting hate speech. While the best-performing models showed impressive results, there is clearly room for improvement in accurately classifying hate speech, particularly in the case of derogatory content. Building on these findings, our team is exploring ways to enhance model performance, including the use of contextualized basics in BERT.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) networks attempt to improve ensemble performance by training separate subnetworks within a base model and combining their predictions. However, these networks have been found to inefficiently use parameters, hindering their adoption and necessitating a larger ensemble size for enhanced performance. This work presents a novel MIMO architecture, dubbed MOE-MIMO, which internalizes ensemble predictions using feature interpolation to minimize parameter redundancy. As a result, MOE-MIMO offers an adaptive way to balance the impact of subnetworks on predictions, achieved through equally weighted feature interpolation in the intermediate layer. The MOE-MIMO architecture also allows the parameter efficiency of individual subnetworks to dictate their contribution to ensemble performance. The benefits of MOE-MIMO are validated through experiments on multi-task classification and clustering tasks, showing the architecture surpasses traditional MIMO networks in both performance and parameter efficiency.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of existing datasets pertinent to the analysis of historical documents through image-based techniques. Specifically, this involves reviewing datasets related to document layout, segmentation, and transcription. Our primary objective is to identify the principal research tasks associated with each dataset, along with their respective domains and the countries of origin, and to examine the sources of these datasets through web search. Furthermore, this research aims to identify potential avenues for expansion by identifying remaining tasks across each domain and country, thereby highlighting areas for further research.

Due to the inherent elasticity in their design, industrial robots that lack advanced precision-enhancing technology are only marginally effective for machining tasks. Besides issues related to structure, temperature, and support bearings, one major factor behind elasticity is the backlash in the transmission systems. This study proposes a method for improving trajectory precision using supplementary sensors and a novel feedback control strategy in combination with a feed-forward approach based on flatness. For this purpose, a novel dynamic model is introduced that accurately describes a flexible robotic joint as a two-mass system subject to dynamic friction. A feed-forward controller is designed to generate optimal torque inputs, and a feedback controller ensures precise tracking by adjusting the joint velocity. This approach has been implemented and tested on an KUKA Quantec KR300 Ultra SE+ robot using a high-precision sensor for real-time monitoring. Comparing the motion trajectories obtained with and without compensation allows for evaluating the compensation effectiveness.

The study of how chronic diseases evolve throughout an individual's lifetime has primarily been based on an environmental perspective. This perspective considers early life experiences and later life social circumstances as interacting components that contribute to future health outcomes. In this context, the concept of 'health pathways' refers to the distinct patterns of health progression observed across different sub-populations. These distinct pathways are driven by various risk factors and are associated with specific health outcomes. A statistical model, the mixed pattern mixture model, was employed to investigate how early life exposures affect the progression of health trajectories. The analysis revealed that early life stress can lead to various future health outcomes, and that certain sociodemographic factors can influence both early life stress levels and future health outcomes. The interaction between early life stress and sociodemographic factors is associated with an increased likelihood of engaging in negative health habits, which in turn affect future health outcomes. The estimates suggest that early life stress can accelerate the progression of health decline by as much as 5 years and can double the likelihood of a health critical pathway. The analysis also indicates that the effects of early life stress on future health outcomes are primarily mediated through intermediate health factors such as body mass index and blood pressure. The estimates show that early life stress can increase the likelihood of a health critical pathway by 30%, and can accelerate the progression of health decline by 3.06 years, and can double the likelihood of a health critical pathway.

One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping grids at each atomic site, effectively dividing the integrand. Although the unaltered Becke scheme exhibits good results, we propose a series of enhancements to support more intricate functions, especially those involving smaller exponents. Our study demonstrates that the modified scheme, combined with a piecewise polynomial representation of the guiding function, yields accurate results and exhibits a convergence pattern consistent with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we apply this method to evaluate hyperintegals and show the approach to be scalable for linear combinations of these and other functions that decline rapidly over distance.

In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if it's possible to uniquely identify each vertex based on the vertices' distinct distances to the chosen set. The problem of finding a resolving set in a subspace subgraph is significant due to its potential applications in metric dimension tasks. However, for general tautology functions, it's unfeasible to determine whether a resolving set exists in subspace subgraphs. In the special case of Taut.functions on 2-dimensional grids, we can confirm the presence of a resolving set within the grid's bounds, and we've developed an algorithm to find such a set in O(n^k) time, where n represents the number of vertices, and k is a constant factor associated with the given tautology function. Additionally, for 1-dimensional grids, the presence of a resolving set can be verified in O(n) time. Furthermore, our research reveals that a novel approach in which we cover the input tautology function with constrained open balls facilitates the identification of a smallest resolving set within these grids. The size of the resulting resolving set closely approximates the optimal, and we've quantified the optimal value in relation to the given tautology function. In the special case of Taut.functions on 2-dimensional grids, we can confirm the optimality of the resulting resolving set within these grids. The size of the resulting resolving set closely approximates the optimal, and we've quantified the optimal value in relation to the given

Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by a self-sustaining system of intense precipitation and cloud cover. The interaction between atmospheric circulation patterns, cloud formation, and water circulation has not been fully understood due to cloud cover's role in limiting surface water evaporation. Recent research has created a simplified model of the water cycle, which treats low-level clouds as separate from the atmosphere and re-allocates water between them and the surface. The model shows that in a stable climate, the water cycle reaches equilibrium and remains stable, but in a simplified 'hothouse' climate, the water cycle becomes unstable and eventually leads to self-sustaining chaos, resulting in irregular and unpredictable atmospheric behavior. The model requires a lower cloud cover to maintain atmospheric equilibrium, but when this cover is present, it causes instability. The model also shows that when a 'hothouse' climate is allowed to develop from a healthy atmosphere, it leads to less cloud cover, which in turn reduces atmospheric instability, however this process is very slow and takes thousands of years, which indicates that the emergence of 'hothouse' climates likely require external factors to disrupt the balance.

We've established an inverse Penrose transform for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variants in a flat space environment. The spin-off variant's twistor action fits within the broader BF framework. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory. This theory's twistor formulation offers a fresh approach to the original self-dual Yang-Mills theory.

The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to its relatively low requirement for pre-existing domain knowledge and ability to derive it from large amounts of data. However, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on large, noise-free datasets, and are often susceptible to errors when dealing with incomplete or imprecise annotations. As a result, their performance in real-world clinical settings is often hindered by the noise introduced during the labeling process, which necessitates the incorporation of additional refinement steps into their workflow. This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of two data augmentation techniques in minimizing the impact of annotation noise on the performance of deep learning-based algorithms in medical image classification tasks. By examining the performance of DNN models with and without these augmentation techniques on various numbers of annotations, our findings highlight the importance of incorporating these steps into the classification process to achieve robust image classification results.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is derived from the Grover walk on a graph G by introducing an interaction term. We establish that on a graph G with a highest eigenvalue of Λ max, the CRW's long-term speed is at most Λ max/2. This upper limit is upheld even if the state space is infinitely large. Furthermore, we present the condition under which the CRW's speed is exactly Λ max/2. Our findings are demonstrated by counteracting an earlier conjecture regarding the unbounded speed of the CRW, as previously suggested by the research of Aizicovski et al.

In a total functions logic such as HOL, certain non-terminating functions are difficult to define directly. To overcome this limitation, a clock mechanism is often introduced to enforce termination, but this can unnecessarily complicate reasoning about properties within the logic. This paper presents an alternative solution, allowing the definition of potentially non-terminating functions without introducing a clock. It achieves this by redefining termination as a dual concept that applies only to functions with a clear completion point, freeing other functions from termination constraints. Additionally, this approach facilitates simplification of clock-based termination analyses in HOL, as well as the reevaluation of its utility in the context of total functions.

The accuracy of model predictions for wall-bounded flow dynamics can be assessed using two key metrics: the amplitude of velocity oscillations near the wall (representing skin-friction drag) and the phase shift of these oscillations (corresponding to wall shear stress). Available statistical models for these metrics show varying degrees of influence from Reynolds number in different types of flow. However, a simplified model applying to a broad range of geometries and flow types, including turbulent and laminar flows, demonstrates a more consistent relationship with high-Reynolds-number conditions. This model shows that the amplitude of velocity oscillations at high Reynolds numbers is primarily controlled by the flow's near-wall velocity gradient and a dimensionless distance measure from the wall. The model's simplicity and consistency at high Reynolds numbers are further validated by its effective prediction of the wall shear stress phase shift.

This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model that incorporates Born-Infeld term governed gauge field behavior. The effective implementation of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework yields an energy lower bound, with corresponding self-dual solutions being derived via an elliptic sine-Gordon equation. We then proceed to analyze the self-dual solutions within a modified baby Skyrme model for three different cases, each involving a non-linear sigma model with a compact or non-compact space, as well as a 2-sphere boundary condition. Furthermore, a numerical investigation is conducted for both smooth (differential) and non-smooth (sharp) geometric boundary conditions applied to the target space manifold.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model in a magnetic field, where each unit cell has an orbital magnetic flux of $p/q$ with $0\le p \le q-1$, we studied its phase diagram under minimal crystalline symmetry. The results showed the existence of various phases: phases exhibiting $q$ type nodes that are linearly dispersive, a phase with a non-zero Chern number, a non-zero Mott insulating phase, and a Higgs phase. In the $q=3$ case, we found that the node configuration can be arranged in three distinct patterns and studied these separately. Furthermore, we explored whether these phases can be achieved in materials like Ta$_3$W$_6$ and WTe$_2$.

This research paper introduces an advanced optical nanoantenna design that maximizes light absorption in emitters while facilitating directed light release. The proposed nanoantenna consists of a complex interaction between a metallic nanosphere and a dielectric metasurface, specifically engineered to maximize light absorption within the emitter and redirect excess light energy into the radiation mode for efficient light release. A detailed study using the recursive green function method within a coupled mode theory revealed that by optimizing the parameters of the nanoantenna, the absorption ratio of the emitter can be precisely fine-tuned, ranging from 94 percent to 99 percent, with correspondingly high radiation efficiency reaching as high as 90 percent. Furthermore, the influence of the meta-surface's losses on the absorption and radiation efficiencies of the emitter was thoroughly examined, showing that high loss densities in the meta-surface can significantly hinder the emitter's absorption capabilities but still allow the emitter to boost light release by redirecting losses outside the radiation mode. The findings of this study offer valuable insights into the capabilities of metal-dielectric nanoantennas as highly efficient light-enhancement devices that promote sustainable light emission from quantum dot, nanowire, and other potential solid-state emitters.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized across solid-state systems.  Nucleation of defects, scars and folds in curved crystals, as well as rearrangements of cells within biological tissue, all exhibit this phenomenon.  A crucial aspect of theoretical models for these systems is the degree to which they can protect the underlying lattice or microscopic structure.  A new study on amorphous solids has demonstrated that mechanical screening can manifest in two distinct forms - a previously proposed version that nearly eliminates deformations or a more recent version that permits some deformations to occur.  Through simulations and theoretical analysis, the researchers found that the two forms of screening arise from fundamentally different mechanisms and are characterized by the presence of a soft mode in the former and a more widespread "cage" mechanism in the latter.  A transition can occur between these two forms of screening when the strain magnitude exceeds a certain threshold.  A new version of the "cage" mechanism that accounts for the absence of quasi-localized modes within the amorphous structure has also been proposed.  Overall, the findings of this study have significant implications for the understanding of mechanical behavior in amorphous solids.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is thoroughly examined.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 million years, to a significantly older, 10 million-year-old oddball. Recent investigations into its central source, however, have uncovered key findings that could help resolve this discrepancy. By examining the light patterns and spectral characteristics of the central source, scientists have determined that it likely comprises a very close, orbiting star near the black hole, as well as a possible jet or plume emanating from the black hole itself. Notably, the source's spectra match a model of a hot bubble perfectly, suggesting the inclusions of iron and other elements within this area. Although the exact identity of the central source remains unclear, its characteristics suggest a scenario where a star is closely orbiting the black hole, producing the energetic emissions observed.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that oversampling significantly enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of KNN and SVM algorithms is heavily influenced by class imbalance issues, whereas random oversampling yields comparable results with minority class oversampling methods.

This study investigates the association between the COVID-19 outbreak in the US and local news coverage, focusing on the interplay between reporting rates and the spread of the virus. Analyzing a comprehensive dataset of 900 US counties from March to October 2020, our research reveals a noteworthy connection between COVID-19 news coverage and national death tolls. Initially, correlation was low but gained significance over time. Moreover, correlation between local news and national cases in some areas was positive, while in others it was negative, albeit statistically insignificant at initial stages. As the pandemic progressed, we observed a clear divide between high and low COVID-19 reporting counties, with the former correlating positively and the latter negatively with national death counts. Our findings also show that the trend of local news coverage was more prominent in counties with later and varying COVID-19 onset dates, underscoring the complex dynamics of the outbreak's progression. Ultimately, our research suggests that the COVID-19 outbreak's spread has been influenced by a combination of factors, with local news coverage playing a notable part in the pandemic's trajectory.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless if the SPH method is accurately applied. However, typical implementations tend to experience minor inaccuracies in conservation, leading to noticeable fluctuations, especially at smaller scales, in courses like numerical analysis. This paper focuses on the causes of non-conservation in SPH implementations, which involve numerical methods in addition to the fundamental SPH framework. By examining a basic scenario with an arbitrary function and considering common kernel types, this study assesses the influence of numerical techniques on conservation properties. An optimal combination of numerical methods for achieving exact conservation of mass, momentum, and energy is identified, which relies on a specific combination of trilinear interpolation and Voronoi discretization. This knowledge can serve as a guideline for developing conserving SPH algorithms.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments measuring the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. Calculations considering a scenario with fully polarized, in-line initial and final protons have been carried out to analyze polarization transfer and compare results to an experiment measuring double-spin asymmetry in another process. Research found a significant $Q^2$ dependence influence on polarization transfer to the proton, which may be exploited in new experiments to measure the $G_E/G_M$ ratio. This also led to proposing an assessment criterion for measurements made using the Rosenbluth technique and applying it to analyze outcomes from multiple studies.

We develop a novel yet efficient learning method that requires minimal data inputs 
and leverages pre-generated synthetic states to accelerate both reinforcement and
imitation learning processes. To achieve this, we utilize the advisor agent to explore
the environment and collect transition samples, which are then combined with synthetic
states to train a policy network using the teacher agent's known policies. As a result,
the teacher agent's preferences can be utilized in black-box imitation learning scenarios 
where behavioral cloning is feasible but the reward function or expert model is unknown.
Moreover, our approach seamlessly integrates with existing promising learning methods to 
boost data efficiency. We conduct comprehensive experiments that validate the proposed
learning strategy on both reinforcement and imitation learning benchmarks, offering 
substantial improvements in performance with minimal additional computational requirements.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) using a massive dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at a 13 TeV energy has been carried out utilizing the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The research explores final states in which the vector boson decays into electrons and neutrinos or into electrons and other electrons and neutrinos, and each Higgs boson decays into pairs of $b$-quarks. It aims to detect the $Vhh$ signals from non-resonant and resonant production of $hh$ pairs, with the latter predicted in certain Standard Model extensions. For the former, a 95% confidence upper limit of 183 times the predicted Standard Model cross-section has been observed, whereas in the latter case, a 95% confidence upper limit of 20 times $R_{hh}$, with $R_{hh}$ defined as the ratio of observed resonant cross-section to predicted Standard Model cross-section, has been set with the assumed mass of $m_{hh}$ equal to 650 GeV. Furthermore, an exclusion upper limit has been set on the resonant production of $m_{hh}$ equal to 710 GeV in the Standard Model.

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities. This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the system to maintain resonance and thus operate efficiently. Our study introduces a simpler method utilizing a phase detector to drive and maintain resonance within these systems, eliminating the need for complex lock-in amplifiers and expansive bandwidth dye-laser systems. Furthermore, we show how this technique enables the system to operate off-resonance, thereby increasing the dynamic range and enabling the system to detect weaker magnetic fields.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between $0$ and $18$ and must be an even integer. Conversely, applying the technique of hypergeometric groups, K3 surface automorphisms possessing Siegel disks can be constructed to demonstrate all conceivable Picard numbers through the identification and computation of relevant algebraic numbers derived from Lefschetz-type formulas and their corresponding residues.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We've introduced an effective Lagrangian to describe this process and establish constraints based on direct dark matter detection experiments and decay rate limits. With these constraints in mind, the remaining parameter space is explored using relic density and antiproton constraints, resulting in a substantial number of parameter combinations that satisfy these conditions. Furthermore, the decaying neutralino scenario is found to outperform the typical dark matter scenarios within the minimal supergravity unified theory, particularly for large Compton wave length ratios of the neutralino and bino. We've also found that future direct dark matter detection experiments will be capable of closing a substantial fraction of the remaining parameter space in future runs. Similarly, the Fermilab Giant Liquid Argon experiment has the potential to explore nearly 70% of the remaining parameter space in proton-proton collisions during the HL-LHC's operation. However, the sensitivity of the future CLIC electron-positron collider will be required to explore around 85% of the remaining parameter space. Therefore, a significant portion of the remaining parameter space will be accessible to future colliders and the dark matter research community will need to adopt a more comprehensive perspective that combines direct dark matter detection, antimatter searches, and long-lived particle signatures in its search for dark matter.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface area packing of squares, and extending this approach to rectangular boxes. Additionally, a 1994 problem proposed by Jockusch and Shore on the computability of binary partition functions can be partially addressed through these findings.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin and, given their limited data, any successful method reduces dependencies on labeled local training data. Our experiment's use of varied architectures, data, and setup evaluations yields comparable results to newer models like BERT, further showcasing the potential for adapting to other low-resource languages.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating background electron recoils triggered by gamma rays from radioactive substances within the detector and surroundings. We created new indicators that can tell electron and nuclear recoils apart at keV-level energies in a model scenario. We also developed a systematic method for generating indicator templates from simulated data. This approach is also applicable to real-time analysis. Our research found that, using the maximum entropy generator algorithm, we can create indicators that can distinguish between the two types of recoils using only the shape of the distributions. Furthermore, using a metric such as the Jensen-Shannon divergence, we can evaluate the effectiveness of these indicators. We can refine these indicators by including additional information in the simulation. We can also analyze how these indicators change in response to variations in the model parameters. We can, for instance, analyze how they change when the ratio of the velocity components is shifted or how the ionization patterns in the detector change. We also discovered that these indicators are highly correlated with the ionization patterns, specifically with the ionization momentum. We propose a method for generating directional

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we propose a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between driving behavior and relevant environmental factors. Based on a systematic review of existing driver-assessment literature, we identified six key components from multiple frameworks that underpin driver assessment. By framing the driver-assessment process as a multi-objective optimization problem, we defined and operationalized each component in relation to identified objectives. By incorporating expert input, we refined our initial results and produced a customized driver-assessment model. However, our knowledge discovery process uncovered critical limitations of relying solely on self-reported data for building driver-assessment models. As a result, we propose the development of an ontology governing the integration of behavioral data and contextual information for accurate driver assessment.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted that existing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models
encounter significant difficulties when encountering unknown text during the training phase.
To address this issue, we evaluated various techniques for handling unseen data.
Notably, our investigation into an extensive dataset comprising 65,000+ unique distinct
scene text instances across 35 languages laid bare the current state of Optical Character
Recognition models in handling unseen data.
Through the competition, we presented BERT-based models that yielded exceptional
results on the challenge dataset, thereby earning the top two accolades in multiple
evaluation categories.

Random fields in mathematics serve as a tool for analyzing functions on high-dimensional spaces that are governed by stochastic processes. Researchers commonly employ random fields for modeling complex systems in various fields, such as engineering, computer graphics, and computer-aided design. A novel non-parametric approach to analyzing random fields via kernel embedding has emerged, allowing for the creation of embedded random fields that can be studied in the context of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. This enables a range of applications including statistical inference, risk assessment, and optimization, often with a focus on tackling machine learning challenges. A recent advancement extended this approach to temporal processes, marking a progression towards addressing temporal modeling issues, which often arise in disciplines like speech and motion planning. This talk will examine non-parametric continuous-time random processes derived through kernelization, providing a continuum between discrete dynamic random variables and static spatial random fields. A key aspect will involve establishing that this kernelization process yields embedded random processes that are consistent across discrete and continuous time domains. This realization will enable novel applications in spatial and temporal modeling, including the novel problem of temporal fields. A related set of outcomes will also be discussed to address the widely recognized challenges in performing cross-domain tasks, such as predicting the future location (or motion planning) given a future but unknown location (or velocity).
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, to the level of locally symmetric spaces for the tree maiximal compact subgroups of $Sp_n(Z)$ and show that its algebraic component at critical point $m$ has bounded denominators as $\chi$ changes. This work refines a previous finding of the first author in 1996 for the case of elliptic curves.

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature. The results show that spin polarization oscillates more intensely in nanoribbons with wider band gaps compared to 2D graphene structures, achieving nearly perfect spin polarization in normal-conductor graphene normal-conductor junctions. The differing electronic properties of normal conductor and graphene materials create confined states in the device that heavily influence transport properties, including conductance and spin polarization. The spin polarization of electrons also oscillates more intensely in monodisperse graphene nanoribbons with varying gate voltages, producing fascinating transport behaviors that could be regulated by adjusting the barrier heights and widths.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a pancyclic structure.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy density, pressure variations, and radial movement along a specific axis, finding significant relationships among these elements. By comparing data on specific particles to laboratory collisions, researchers discovered that an initial medium imbalance is a primary driver of light particles' trajectory. The uneven initial medium creates opposite forces depending on impact point and rapidity direction, causing a negative trajectory for light particles. The trajectory of the heaviest particles, such as deuterons and tritons, is unaffected by this imbalance due to their charge. The study also showed that a global medium shift and collective flow play minor roles in explaining the directed flow of light particles, and that the medium's viscosity has a negligible effect on the measured data. The study further found that an analysis that takes into account the movement and distribution changes of the medium along a rapidity line and the corresponding energy density variations can accurately explain the directed flow of different particles, including deuterons, antiprotons, and pions.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as boundary conditions for other problems. Despite its initial two-dimensional applications, the method has been extended to solve high-dimensional systems. However, standard ASK relies on a collocation time integration technique that uses a high number of time steps, resulting in a high computational cost. To reduce this cost, the ASK method has been modified to use a sparse grid approach to minimize the number of time steps and collocation points. In this study, the effectiveness of the sparse-grid-based ASK method was tested on two important mathematical models: a multi-dimensional nonlinear system and a model for biological cell dynamics. The results show that the sparse-grid-based ASK method reduces the computational cost of time integration, allowing for more efficient numerical solutions of multi-dimensional dynamical systems.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical difficulties in explaining ionization within the framework of quantum mechanics. The fundamental principles of resonance theory are then explored and its application to the description of quasistable states, especially in the context of highly excited atoms and molecules, is examined in detail. The review also highlights the significant contributions of the renowned theorist Vladimir Fock to this field and includes a thorough analysis of his work on resonance parameters and their practical application. An outline is also given for a new approach to analyzing quantum-kinetic properties, a perspective which was strongly influenced by the work and ideas of Vladimir Fock.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes may result in degenerate scenarios where the solution does not exist, research demonstrates that even in such situations, the Sinkhorn algorithm leads to two specific points of convergence. Crucially, these limit points enable the calculation of a solution to a more relaxed version of the original problem. The relaxed version can be thought of as the result of replacing the original problem's marginal constraints with marginal penalizations in a related problem. As a result of this finding, a new theoretical connection between two types of probabilistic models has been established, which will be further explored in upcoming research.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recently recorded data of top-quark pair production in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV center-of-mass energy, which yielded a comprehensive dataset of 421 million pairs of events. This measurement utilizes the full integrated luminosity, equivalent to 1.06 fb^-1, to establish a precise differential cross-section with an accuracy of 5%. By employing a likelihood-based fit method to account for background influences from diboson, diphoton final states and multijet backgrounds, the majority of systematic uncertainties can be effectively mitigated. Furthermore, this analysis adheres to a rigorous validation procedure to ensure the accuracy of the likelihood-based fit. With these advancements, the study provides precise differential cross-section measurements that can be used to constrain parton distribution functions and to make precise predictions about top-quark pair production in future calculations, potentially down to 1.5%.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this phenomenon in the context of systems involving multiple interacting particles coupled with a central qubit or cavity, which are gaining attention in various experimental platforms. There's also an interesting link between these systems and the phenomenon of Floquet many-body localization, which occurs when the external influence is treated as a quantifiable drive. We've applied the multilayer multiconfigurational time-dependent Hartree method to simulate the dynamic interactions between a central degree of freedom - represented as a multilevel system - and a one-dimensional disordered interacting quantum system served as a controllable bath. This allowed us to model not only the core system's behavior but also the co-evolving system's state. We observed the emergence of distinct patterns of long-lived oscillations within the core system and the formation of long-lived autocoherent fields on the bath when we chose specific parameters that lead to the formation of a localised phase at the core system. We have also studied in detail the effects of varying the coupling strength between the core system and the bath. Our results could potentially contribute to a deeper understanding of the core system's dynamics that is not completely determined by its properties alone and may open new avenues to control the core system's behavior through the adjustment of the surrounding system.

${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${|u}_{p,b,c}(z)|<|z|$ for all $z$ within a specific region, and the conditions are also specified that would make the function the best dominant function in a set of generalized Bessel functions within that region. Several open problems are posed.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates nearing pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, the research suggests that the pandemic exacerbated social distancing norms among certain groups, largely affecting diversity of encounters in urban environments.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Multiplicative Schwarz Newton, operates in a sequential two-step process:
initially addressing capillary forces and secondly dealing with the effects of
advection. This approach is evaluated against a conventional Newton-Krylov
method utilizing a monolithic formulation of the problem. Subsequent numerical
experiments indicate the FSMP method effectively minimizes computational time. 
Moreover, to optimize spatial non-homogeneity, a finite volume framework with
variable grid sizes according to the phase concentrations of substances has been
established. This approach offers efficient processing by distributing computational
tasks in parallel, utilizing MPI for communication. In comparison to the Newton-Krylov
method, the FSMP algorithm demonstrates a notable reduction in the required number
of iterations for convergence. A more in-depth, two-phase flow and transport
study shows FSMP's superiority in achieving convergence with fewer function
evaluations.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various fields, encompassing the arrangement of molecular structures, spin orientation, and circular polarization of light.  A pioneering approach to optical isolation utilizing magneto-optical Kerr effect-based technology has been proposed to discriminate between left- and right-handed forms of chiral molecules.  If an incoming light beam is of the left-handed or right-handed circular polarization type, it is anticipated that the refractive index will be affected in a manner exhibiting non-reciprocal properties.  This concept offers a promising means of achieving optical isolation using available technology.  Notably, the required magneto-optical Kerr effect can be provided by thin film structures comprising a birefringent material in close proximity to a planar magneto-optical layer, such as a Co ferrite or a GdFeCo alloy.  This combination can achieve a sufficient Kerr rotation for effective optical isolation.  The working principle of this unit is based on the modulation of light refractive index in response to applied magnetic fields, thereby enabling the construction of optical half-wave and polarization rotator devices.  These devices can perform functions such as circular to linear conversion of light polarization and vice versa.  Furthermore, the employed thin film technology facilitates the development of standardized fabrication protocols to ensure reliable optical isolation.  The resulting optical half-wave plate device can accomplish a range of functions, including circular to linear conversion of light polarization and vice versa.
